questions.q: On what date in 1955 was Rosa Parks arrested in Montgomery, Alabama, for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white passenger?
questions.explain: Her arrest on December 1, 1955 led local leaders to call a bus boycott that began the following Monday, December 5.

questions.q: How long did the Montgomery bus boycott last before King called for its end on December 20, 1956?
questions.explain: The boycott began on December 5, 1955, and ran for about thirteen months, until the buses were integrated after a Supreme Court ruling.

questions.q: Which organization, formed on December 5, 1955, chose Martin Luther King Jr. as its president to lead the Montgomery bus boycott?
questions.explain: The MIA was created the day the boycott began. The SCLC followed in 1957, after the boycott showed what organized protest could do.

questions.q: Which Montgomery leader, president of the Women's Political Council, organized the printing and distribution of leaflets calling for the 1955 bus boycott?
questions.explain: Robinson prepared the leaflets at Alabama State College, and her council helped distribute them.

questions.q: Which longtime Montgomery NAACP leader helped arrange Rosa Parks's bail and phoned local ministers to plan the boycott?
questions.explain: Nixon, a former head of the local NAACP branch, helped bring the city's ministers into the protest.

questions.q: About what share of Montgomery's Black residents stayed off the buses on the first day of the boycott, December 5, 1955?
questions.explain: Organizers were surprised by the turnout, because the buses ran nearly empty of Black riders that first morning.

questions.q: In which case did a federal district court rule on June 5, 1956, that bus segregation in Montgomery was unconstitutional, a decision the Supreme Court later affirmed?
questions.explain: Browder v. Gayle, brought by Montgomery women, ended the boycott once the Supreme Court affirmed the ruling in November 1956.

questions.q: After being convicted for his role in the Montgomery boycott, King was ordered to pay a $500 fine or serve how many days in jail?
questions.explain: More than 80 boycott leaders were indicted under a 1921 anti-boycott law, and King's conviction was for his part in organizing the protest.

questions.q: Where was the founding meeting of the SCLC held in January 1957?
options: Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery
Sixth Avenue Baptist Church in Birmingham
questions.explain: The meeting, called the Southern Negro Leaders Conference on Transportation and Nonviolent Integration, met at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta.

questions.q: SCLC staff member Dorothy Cotton became best known for what kind of work?
options: Training local communities in nonviolence and leadership through citizenship schools
Writing the legal briefs for the Montgomery bus boycott lawsuits
Managing the 1963 March on Washington's program of speakers
Negotiating the Birmingham settlement with city business leaders
questions.explain: Cotton helped run SCLC's citizenship education work, which taught people to organize and pass voter registration tests.

questions.q: What was the main goal of the SCLC's 1957 Crusade for Citizenship?
options: Ending segregation on interstate buses and trains
Registering Black voters who had been shut out of the electorate
Starting a national campaign of lunch counter sit-ins
Building Black-owned banks and businesses across the South
questions.explain: The crusade held voter education clinics across the South to register disenfranchised citizens.

questions.q: On what date in 1963 did Martin Luther King Jr. write his Letter from Birmingham Jail?
questions.explain: King wrote it in his cell four days after his April 12 arrest, answering clergymen who had criticized the Birmingham protests.

questions.q: King's Letter from Birmingham Jail answered a public statement by eight Birmingham clergy who called the demonstrations what?
questions.explain: Eight Birmingham clergymen issued the statement, which a local newspaper published; King answered it in his letter written from jail.

questions.q: On April 12, 1963, King was arrested in Birmingham for violating what?
options: A state court injunction against demonstrations
A city ordinance against loitering at bus terminals
A state law banning interracial assembly in churches
A federal order against interstate travel
questions.explain: A state circuit court had issued an injunction against protests on April 10; King chose to march anyway on Good Friday and was jailed.

questions.q: Which list gives the four basic steps of a nonviolent campaign that King laid out in the Letter from Birmingham Jail?
options: Petition, boycott, lawsuit and new legislation
Prayer, fasting, picketing and voluntary arrest
Collecting the facts, negotiation, self-purification and direct action
Voter registration, education, organization and election
questions.explain: King argued Birmingham's activists had followed every step, so the charge that they acted too soon did not hold.

questions.q: In 1964 King reworked the Letter from Birmingham Jail as a chapter of which book?
options: Where Do We Go from Here
questions.explain: Why We Can't Wait told the story of the 1963 Birmingham campaign and included the revised Letter.

questions.q: Which SCLC leader was arrested together with King on April 12, 1963, in Birmingham?
questions.explain: Abernathy, King's close friend and later SCLC president, shared the Birmingham jail with him.

questions.q: The 1963 Birmingham campaign ended with a settlement announced on which date?
questions.explain: Leaders announced the settlement on May 10, after the campaign that had begun on April 3.

questions.q: Which Birmingham commissioner of public safety ordered police and fire departments to use force against demonstrators in May 1963?
questions.explain: Connor's use of fire hoses and police dogs against young marchers was shown across the United States and abroad.

questions.q: Which minister founded the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights, SCLC's local partner in the Birmingham campaign?
questions.explain: Shuttlesworth was hit by a fire hose while leading young marchers and was hospitalized, but he joined King to announce the settlement.

questions.q: What happened after more than 1,000 students tried to march downtown in Birmingham on May 2, 1963, that shocked audiences worldwide?
options: The mayor ordered the schools closed for the rest of the year
The Alabama National Guard shot tear gas into the Sixth Avenue church
Federal marshals arrested the students for truancy and sedition
Police used high-pressure fire hoses and dogs against young marchers
questions.explain: Hundreds of children were arrested, and images of them under fire hoses and dog attacks built pressure for a settlement.

questions.q: Which was among the terms of the May 1963 Birmingham settlement?
options: Removing "Whites Only" and "Blacks Only" signs and desegregating lunch counters
Immediate desegregation of every Birmingham public school
A federal takeover of the city police department
A new state law banning segregated housing
questions.explain: The settlement also called for upgrading Black employment, a biracial committee and release of jailed protesters on bond.

questions.q: In September 1963, Klansmen bombed the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham. How many young girls were killed?
questions.explain: The bombing on September 15, 1963, killed four girls and deepened national support for a federal civil rights law.

questions.q: After bombings followed the Birmingham settlement, President Kennedy ordered about how many federal troops into position near the city?
questions.explain: Kennedy also prepared to federalize the Alabama National Guard if the violence continued.

questions.q: Which candidate defeated Bull Connor in a Birmingham runoff for mayor, a result that preceded the start of the 1963 campaign?
questions.explain: Boutwell defeated Connor in the April 2, 1963, runoff, the day before the Birmingham demonstrations began.

questions.q: Which organizer served as deputy director of the 1963 March on Washington and handled much of its planning?
questions.explain: Rustin pulled together an event for more than 200,000 people in about two months.

questions.q: Which labor leader, founder of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, was a leading figure behind the 1963 March on Washington?
questions.explain: Randolph, who first proposed a march on Washington in 1941, was director of the 1963 march.

questions.q: What did John Lewis agree to cut from his draft speech at the 1963 march after other leaders objected to its tone?
options: A vow to march through the South like Sherman's army
A tribute to the Freedom Riders of 1961
A request for a new federal jobs program
A criticism of the Supreme Court's Brown decision
questions.explain: Lewis softened phrases about marching through the South, but still voiced SNCC's reservations about President Kennedy's civil rights bill.

questions.q: John Lewis spoke at the 1963 March on Washington as chairman of which organization?
questions.explain: Lewis spoke for SNCC, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, which had chosen him as its chairman earlier in 1963. He was the youngest speaker at the march.

questions.q: Which group was among the original sponsors of the 1963 march, along with the Negro American Labor Council, SCLC and CORE?
questions.explain: The NAACP, Urban League, National Council of Churches and UAW joined later as participants or sponsors.

questions.q: Which was among the stated goals of the 1963 March on Washington?
options: Reparations for descendants of enslaved people
A constitutional amendment ending the Electoral College
A federal Fair Employment Practices Act
A ban on nuclear weapons testing
questions.explain: Its goals also included a comprehensive civil rights bill, voting rights protection and school desegregation.

questions.q: After the 1963 march, King and other leaders met at the White House with President Kennedy and which other official?
questions.explain: Johnson would sign the Civil Rights Act into law less than a year later.

questions.q: Which organization, through spokesman Malcolm X, condemned the 1963 March on Washington, though Malcolm X attended it?
questions.explain: The group condemned the march, though Malcolm X himself attended it.

questions.q: Which contralto, who had sung on the Lincoln Memorial steps in 1939, appeared again at the 1963 march?
questions.explain: Anderson's 1939 concert had made the memorial a symbol of the fight against segregation, and she returned in 1963.

questions.q: Whose shooting by an Alabama state trooper on February 18, 1965, helped spark the Selma marches?
questions.explain: Jackson, a 26-year-old church deacon from Marion, died eight days later in a Selma hospital.

questions.q: Which young SNCC leader suffered a fractured skull on Bloody Sunday, March 7, 1965?
questions.explain: Lewis, later a member of Congress, was struck on the head by a state trooper at the Edmund Pettus Bridge.

questions.q: On March 9, 1965, King led more than 2,000 marchers to the Edmund Pettus Bridge, knelt in prayer and turned back. Why?
options: To avoid defying a pending federal court order
Because Governor Wallace had agreed to negotiate
Because troopers had blocked the road with barricades
Because the marchers had run out of food and water
questions.explain: The turnaround angered some younger activists but kept the movement on the right side of the court while it sought permission.

questions.q: James Reeb, a white minister beaten in Selma on March 9, 1965, who died two days later, belonged to which denomination?
questions.explain: Reeb had come from Massachusetts to join the Selma protests, and his death added to calls for a federal voting law.

questions.q: Which famous phrase did President Johnson declare in his March 15, 1965, address to Congress urging a voting rights law?
options: "Ask not what your country can do for you"
"The only thing we have to fear"
questions.explain: Johnson borrowed the anthem of the movement and told Congress that the demonstrators' cause "must be our cause too."

questions.q: How long was the final march from Selma to Montgomery, completed between March 21 and 25, 1965?
questions.explain: Marchers covered 7 to 17 miles a day under federal protection and camped in supporters' yards.

questions.q: About how large had the Selma to Montgomery march crowd grown by its final day, when King spoke at the Alabama capitol?
questions.explain: The marchers narrowed to about 300 on the two-lane stretch of highway, then swelled to about 25,000 by the time they reached Montgomery.

questions.q: Which Michigan volunteer was shot and killed by Ku Klux Klan members on the night of March 25, 1965, while shuttling marchers back to Selma?
questions.explain: Federal prosecutors later convicted three Klansmen of conspiring to violate her civil rights.

questions.q: On what date did President Johnson sign the Voting Rights Act, with King and other leaders present?
questions.explain: Johnson signed the act in the Capitol's President's Room, with King and other leaders looking on.

questions.q: What did Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 require of covered states and counties?
options: A new census of all voting-age residents every five years
Poll watchers from the state at every polling place
Federal approval before putting new voting rules into effect
Public funding of every candidate's campaign
questions.explain: This preclearance requirement was a central tool until the Supreme Court struck down the coverage formula in 2013.

questions.q: The Voting Rights Act's coverage formula applied where a test or device was in use on November 1, 1964, and fewer than what share of voting-age residents were registered or voted in that year's election?
questions.explain: Jurisdictions meeting both conditions were subject to special federal oversight of their voting laws.

questions.q: About how many new Black voters had been registered by the end of 1965, with one-third of them signed up by federal examiners?
questions.explain: The act produced a quick change in registration, especially in counties where federal examiners were sent.

questions.q: Which 1966 Supreme Court case upheld key provisions of the Voting Rights Act against a challenge by South Carolina?
questions.explain: The Court upheld Section 5 and the preclearance system it created.

questions.q: Congress renewed the Voting Rights Act several times. Which set lists three of those renewal years?
questions.explain: Congress also renewed it in 2006; the 2013 Shelby County ruling struck down the coverage formula.

questions.q: On what date did President Johnson sign the Civil Rights Act that outlawed segregation in public accommodations?
questions.explain: King and other civil rights leaders were present when Johnson signed the law that outlawed segregation in public accommodations.

questions.q: In a nationally broadcast speech on June 11, 1963, which president announced he would send Congress a comprehensive civil rights bill?
questions.explain: Kennedy said the nation "will not be fully free until all its citizens are free" and submitted the bill on June 19.

questions.q: For roughly how long did Southern senators filibuster the Civil Rights Act of 1964 before the Senate voted to end debate in June?
questions.explain: Cloture was invoked on June 10, 1964, and the bill passed the Senate on June 19.

questions.q: Which agency did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 create to address race and sex discrimination in employment?
questions.explain: The EEOC still investigates workplace discrimination complaints today.

questions.q: The Civil Rights Act of 1957 was notable as the first civil rights law passed by Congress since when?
questions.explain: It created the Civil Rights Division of the Justice Department and a U.S. Civil Rights Commission.

questions.q: On what date did the Supreme Court decide Brown v. Board of Education, unanimously ruling that segregated public schools were unconstitutional?
questions.explain: Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote that separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.

questions.q: The Brown decision combined cases from Kansas and which three other places?
questions.explain: The Topeka case gave the ruling its name, but it grouped four lawsuits.

questions.q: Where did King accept the Nobel Peace Prize on December 10, 1964?
questions.explain: Gunnar Jahn, chairman of the Nobel Committee, presented the prize in Oslo.

questions.q: King's Nobel Peace Prize came with about $54,000. What did he do with the money?
options: He put it into a college fund for his four children
He bought a house for the SCLC in Atlanta
He returned it to the Nobel committee in protest
He gave it to the civil rights movement
questions.explain: King said he would turn over the prize money to the civil rights movement.

questions.q: Which organization, a Quaker group that had won the Peace Prize in 1947, nominated King for the 1964 prize?
options: The Gandhi Society for Human Rights
questions.explain: The Quaker service group had itself won the Peace Prize in 1947.

questions.q: In April 1967, King called the Nobel Peace Prize a what when he spoke out against the Vietnam War?
questions.explain: In the Beyond Vietnam speech, King said the prize gave him a duty to speak for peace.

questions.q: At which New York church did King deliver his April 4, 1967, speech opposing the Vietnam War?
questions.explain: The speech, sponsored by Clergy and Laymen Concerned About Vietnam, came exactly one year before his death.

questions.q: Which historian and activist wrote the draft of King's "Beyond Vietnam" speech?
questions.explain: Harding wrote the speech, which called the U.S. the greatest purveyor of violence in the world.

questions.q: How did major newspapers such as The New York Times and The Washington Post react to King's Beyond Vietnam speech?
options: They endorsed it as a historic statement
They called for the Nobel Prize to be revoked
They criticized it as a mistake
questions.explain: The NAACP also criticized the speech, and King lost support among white allies, including President Johnson.

questions.q: On what date did King and the SCLC announce the Poor People's Campaign at a press conference in Atlanta?
questions.explain: The campaign was planned at an SCLC staff retreat in Frogmore, South Carolina, that began in late November 1967, and it was announced publicly days later.

questions.q: Which leader took over the Poor People's Campaign as SCLC president after King's assassination?
questions.explain: Abernathy led the campaign to Washington, where marchers built a shantytown on the Mall.

questions.q: What was the name of the temporary settlement of tents and shacks built on the National Mall by the Poor People's Campaign in 1968?
questions.explain: Protesters lived there for more than a month before the Interior Department closed it on June 24, 1968.

questions.q: Who led the first wave of women on Mother's Day, May 12, 1968, to open the Poor People's Campaign?
questions.explain: Thousands of women marched in Washington in the campaign's opening event, only weeks after her husband's death.

questions.q: Which was one concrete result of the Poor People's Campaign?
options: Two hundred counties qualified for free surplus food
A national minimum wage of two dollars
The creation of the Department of Housing and Urban Development
questions.explain: Federal agencies also promised to hire poor people, though SCLC's leaders considered the gains inadequate.

questions.q: What event on February 1, 1968, led to the Memphis sanitation strike?
options: A city worker was shot during a protest at city hall
Mayor Loeb fired every Black employee in the department
Two garbage collectors were crushed to death by a malfunctioning truck
A union organizer was arrested for refusing to testify
questions.explain: Echol Cole and Robert Walker died in the accident, and the workers' demands for safety and union recognition followed.

questions.q: What did strikers' signs say as they marched daily in Memphis in 1968?
questions.explain: The signs asserted the workers' dignity as much as their wages and union rights.

questions.q: Which speech did King deliver at the Mason Temple in Memphis on April 3, 1968, the night before he was killed?
questions.explain: In the speech, King spoke of having seen the promised land, words many listeners later heard as a premonition.

questions.q: Which union granted the Memphis sanitation workers a charter in 1964 and supported their strike under its president Jerry Wurf?
options: The Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters
The American Federation of State, County, and Municipal Employees
questions.explain: AFSCME's support gave the strike organizational and financial backing.

questions.q: Who was the Memphis mayor who refused to recognize the sanitation workers' union in 1968?
questions.explain: Loeb had taken office in January 1968 and rejected a City Council vote to recognize the union.

questions.q: At what site in Memphis was Martin Luther King Jr. shot on April 4, 1968?
questions.explain: He was standing on the second-floor balcony outside room 306 when he was struck at 6:01 p.m.

questions.q: How old was King when he died on April 4, 1968?
questions.explain: He was born January 15, 1929, and was pronounced dead at St. Joseph's Hospital at 7:05 p.m.

questions.q: Which man pleaded guilty to King's murder on March 10, 1969, and was sentenced to 99 years in prison?
questions.explain: Ray had escaped from a Missouri prison in 1967 and was arrested in London in June 1968. He recanted his plea days later.

questions.q: After King's death, President Johnson declared April 7, 1968, to be what?
options: A federal holiday for the Senate
A day of national prayer and fasting
questions.explain: Riots broke out in more than 100 cities, and King's funeral took place in Atlanta on April 9.

questions.q: In 1999, a Memphis civil jury in a lawsuit brought by the King family found what?
options: That James Earl Ray acted alone
That the FBI had planned the shooting
That Loyd Jowers and others were part of a conspiracy
That the Memphis police had fired the rifle
questions.explain: The jury awarded the family $100, though the Justice Department in 2000 said the findings lacked evidence.

questions.q: When was Martin Luther King Jr. Day first observed as a federal holiday?
questions.explain: Congress passed the holiday law in 1983, and the first observance was held three years later.

questions.q: Which president signed the bill creating the federal holiday honoring King on November 2, 1983?
questions.explain: The Senate had passed the bill 78 to 22 and the House 338 to 90 that year.

questions.q: Which musician released the 1980 song "Happy Birthday" to promote the campaign for a King holiday?
questions.explain: The song was part of a campaign that gathered six million signatures on a petition to Congress.

questions.q: The national day of service that follows the King holiday, created by Harris Wofford and John Lewis, was signed into law in which year?
questions.explain: Bill Clinton signed the King Holiday and Service Act in August 1994, and AmeriCorps coordinates the day nationally.

questions.q: At what age did King enter Morehouse College after passing its entrance exam?
questions.explain: He entered in 1944 and graduated with a sociology degree in 1948 at 19.

questions.q: At which seminary did King earn a Bachelor of Divinity in 1951?
questions.explain: He then went on to earn a doctorate at Boston University in 1955.

questions.q: At which Montgomery church was King pastor when the bus boycott began?
questions.explain: King was pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, where he had been called to the pulpit in 1954 at age 25. The boycott began in December 1955.

questions.q: What was King's name at birth in January 1929?
questions.explain: His father later changed both their names to honor the German Protestant reformer Martin Luther.

questions.q: Which Black member of the House of Representatives began introducing the King holiday bill in 1968, shortly after the assassination?
questions.explain: Conyers, a Democrat from Michigan, led the effort in the House.

questions.q: Who was elected the first chairman of SNCC after its founding at Shaw University in 1960?
questions.explain: Barry, a Fisk University student, was elected SNCC's first chairman in May 1960.

questions.q: Which experienced organizer invited student sit-in leaders to the April 1960 Raleigh meeting that founded SNCC and urged them to stay independent?
questions.explain: Baker, an SCLC official and longtime organizer, believed young people should lead their own movement.

questions.q: In May 1966, who was elected SNCC chairman and began calling for "Black Power" during a march in Mississippi?
questions.explain: The new slogan strained SNCC's ties with moderate allies and white supporters.

questions.q: In what year and city was the Congress of Racial Equality founded?
questions.explain: A racially mixed group of students formed CORE, with ties to the Fellowship of Reconciliation.

questions.q: What was the Journey of Reconciliation of 1947, organized by CORE?
options: An integrated bus ride through the upper South to test a ruling against segregated interstate travel
A march from Selma to Montgomery to protest voting restrictions
A boycott of segregated department stores in Atlanta
A sit-in at a Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro
questions.explain: It was a model for the 1961 Freedom Rides, and several riders were sentenced to a North Carolina chain gang.

questions.q: On what date did the Freedom Rides begin, with riders leaving Washington, D.C., aboard two buses bound for New Orleans?
questions.explain: CORE organized the rides to test integration of bus terminals in the Deep South.

questions.q: Where in Alabama was a Freedom Rider bus firebombed on May 14, 1961?
questions.explain: A white mob attacked the passengers who fled the burning bus.

questions.q: Which Nashville student leader argued that the Freedom Rides could not stop because of violence, or the movement would die?
questions.explain: Nash organized replacement riders after the Alabama attacks so that the rides would continue.

questions.q: After the Freedom Rides, an Interstate Commerce Commission ruling banning segregation in interstate bus facilities took effect on what date?
questions.explain: Attorney General Robert Kennedy petitioned the ICC on May 29, 1961; the commission issued its ruling in September, and it took effect November 1.

questions.q: Which three civil rights workers were killed in Mississippi during the summer of 1964?
options: Medgar Evers, Herbert Lee and Emmett Till
Jimmie Lee Jackson, James Reeb and Viola Liuzzo
Vernon Dahmer, Louis Allen and Lamar Smith
James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner
questions.explain: The three young men were working on voter registration with CORE and the Freedom Summer project.

questions.q: Fannie Lou Hamer was the youngest of how many children of Mississippi sharecroppers?
questions.explain: She grew up on a plantation in Sunflower County and became a voting rights leader.

questions.q: Hamer was beaten in a jail in which Mississippi town in 1963, leaving her with lasting kidney and eye damage?
questions.explain: Fannie Lou Hamer, already a SNCC field secretary, and other activists were arrested and beaten in the jail at Winona, Mississippi, in June 1963. The beating left her with lasting kidney and eye damage.

questions.q: Hamer helped organize which group, which challenged Mississippi's all-white delegation at the 1964 Democratic convention?
questions.explain: The party offered a compromise of two at-large seats that Hamer rejected.

questions.q: In 1964 Hamer testified to the Democratic convention in Atlantic City about the violence she had suffered. How did she close her testimony?
options: "If the Freedom Democratic Party is not seated now, I question America."
"I have a dream that one day Mississippi will rise up."
questions.explain: Her televised testimony brought national attention to the party's challenge.

questions.q: Bayard Rustin joined which pacifist organization as a field secretary and later as its race relations director?
options: The Southern Conference for Human Welfare
questions.explain: Rustin also co-founded CORE and helped teach King about Gandhian nonviolence.

questions.q: In 1948 Bayard Rustin traveled to which country to study the philosophy of nonviolence?
questions.explain: He later advised King on nonviolence, a subject King had known mostly from reading.

questions.q: Why did some civil rights leaders urge King to keep his distance from Bayard Rustin?
options: Rustin was openly gay and had once belonged to the Young Communist League
Rustin had criticized the Montgomery boycott
Rustin had refused to attend the Birmingham campaign
Rustin supported Black Power over nonviolence
questions.explain: Rustin's 1953 arrest on a morals charge and his earlier ties to the Young Communist League made him a target, yet he still organized the 1963 march.

questions.q: John Lewis was born in 1940 near which Alabama town, where his parents were sharecroppers?
questions.explain: He first heard King on the radio and began preaching as a teenager.

questions.q: Which Nashville minister led the direct action workshops that trained John Lewis and other students before the 1960 sit-ins?
questions.explain: Lawson's workshops taught Gandhian nonviolence to a generation of student activists.

questions.q: Whom did John Lewis defeat in the 1986 Democratic primary runoff on his way to being elected to the House of Representatives?
questions.explain: Lewis, a former SNCC chairman, served in the House from 1987 until his death in 2020.

questions.q: Rosa Parks served as secretary of which organization's Montgomery branch at the time of her arrest?
questions.explain: Rosa Parks was secretary of the Montgomery branch of the NAACP, which she had joined in 1943. Her arrest in December 1955 sparked the Montgomery bus boycott.

questions.q: In the summer of 1955, Rosa Parks attended a workshop at which Tennessee school on implementing the Supreme Court's desegregation decision?
questions.explain: Septima Clark, who encouraged Parks there, joined the school's staff the following year.

questions.q: After the boycott, Rosa Parks moved to which city to find work, later joining the staff of Representative John Conyers?
questions.explain: She faced harassment in Montgomery and worked in Conyers's office until she retired in 1988.

questions.q: Which sculptor from China created the Stone of Hope statue of King at the national memorial?
questions.explain: Lei was announced as the sculptor in 2007 and carved the figure from 159 blocks of granite.

questions.q: The King memorial's centerpiece takes its form from which line of his "I Have a Dream" speech?
options: "Out of the mountain of despair, a stone of hope"
"The arc of the moral universe is long"
questions.explain: Two granite pieces form the "Mountain of Despair," and the figure of King emerges from the "Stone of Hope."

questions.q: The King memorial design was chosen from about 900 entries. Which San Francisco firm won?
questions.explain: ROMA Design Group's design was selected in 2000, and Ed Jackson Jr. served as executive architect.

questions.q: The curved inscription wall at the King memorial is how long, and how many quotations from King does it carry?
questions.explain: The crescent-shaped granite wall is lined with excerpts from King's sermons, speeches and writings.

questions.q: What fraternity, to which King belonged, first proposed building a memorial to him in Washington?
questions.explain: Fraternity members proposed the memorial in 1984, and Congress authorized it in 1996.

questions.q: The King memorial stands on about four acres at the northwest corner of which body of water in West Potomac Park?
questions.explain: The memorial occupies a site in West Potomac Park on the Tidal Basin.

questions.q: What was the subject of the controversy over an inscription on the Stone of Hope, which led Interior Secretary Ken Salazar to order a correction in 2012?
options: A paraphrased quotation taken from King's "Drum Major Instinct" sermon
A misspelled version of King's name
A date given incorrectly for the March on Washington
A quotation attributed to King that he never said
questions.explain: Critics, including Maya Angelou, said the shortened wording made King sound arrogant; the inscription was removed in 2013.

questions.q: What was the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial's address, which refers to a landmark law?
questions.explain: The Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial's address is 1964 Independence Avenue SW, a street number that echoes the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

questions.q: Which president was the first to address the NAACP, speaking at the Lincoln Memorial on June 29, 1947?
questions.explain: Truman's speech at the memorial was broadcast nationally and called for federal action on civil rights.

questions.q: Why did the Daughters of the American Revolution's refusal to let Marian Anderson sing at Constitution Hall in 1939 lead to a concert at the Lincoln Memorial?
options: Eleanor Roosevelt hosted the concert at the White House
The Library of Congress opened its Great Hall to Anderson
Harold Ickes arranged an open-air Easter concert on the memorial's steps
Congress passed a resolution moving the concert to the Capitol
questions.explain: About 75,000 people came to the Easter Sunday concert in 1939.

questions.q: What kind of weapon did Booth use to shoot Lincoln?
questions.explain: The small pistol held one round, which is why Booth also carried a knife.

questions.q: At what time did Lincoln die after being shot at Ford's Theatre?
questions.explain: He lay unconscious for about nine hours in a house across the street before dying the next morning.

questions.q: Why was Lincoln laid diagonally across the bed in the Petersen House?
options: The doctors needed room to operate on both sides
The bed was a child's bed
His wound required his head to be higher than his feet
He was 6 feet 4 inches tall and the bed was too short
questions.explain: The small bed could not hold his full length in a straight line.

questions.q: Who, as Lincoln died at the Petersen House, set up a temporary office in the back parlor to question witnesses and start the manhunt?
questions.explain: Stanton took charge of the response and met Cabinet members about the transfer of power.

questions.q: Which line is attributed to Edwin Stanton after Lincoln's death, though witnesses disagreed on one word?
questions.explain: Some accounts record the last word as "angels," so historians treat the exact wording as uncertain.

questions.q: The Petersen House was built about 1849 by William and Anna Petersen, immigrants from which country?
questions.explain: William and Anna Petersen were German immigrants; William was a tailor. They ran the house as a family home and boarding house, where Lincoln died in 1865.

questions.q: What distinction did the Petersen House gain in 1896, when the U.S. government bought it?
options: It was the first time the federal government bought a historic house for preservation
It became the first museum run by the Smithsonian
It became the first site listed as a national shrine by Congress
It became the first home to be moved to the National Mall
questions.explain: The government purchase came decades before the National Park Service took over care of the house.

questions.q: Who photographed the inside of the Petersen House in 1865, taking the only known photographs of the room?
options: The Ulke brothers, renters in the house
questions.explain: Henry and Julius Ulke were renters who entered the room after Lincoln's body was removed.

questions.q: Where is the bed on which Lincoln died now kept?
options: The Smithsonian National Museum of American History
questions.explain: The Petersen House is furnished with period pieces, but none of its furnishings is original to the house.

questions.q: Who treated Lincoln first in Ford's Theatre, a young Army surgeon who found the wound behind his left ear?
questions.explain: Leale was a young Union Army surgeon who found the wound behind Lincoln's left ear.

questions.q: Which actress, the star of Our American Cousin that night, is reported by several witnesses to have cradled the dying president’s head in the box at Ford's Theatre?
questions.explain: Laura Keene starred in Our American Cousin; Dr. Charles Leale and others said she held Lincoln’s head, though some witnesses disputed that she was ever in the box.

questions.q: Which army officer, a guest in Lincoln's box, was stabbed by Booth as he tried to stop him?
questions.explain: Rathbone had come with his fiancee, Clara Harris, as guests of the Lincolns.

questions.q: What happened to Booth as he jumped from the presidential box to the stage?
options: He was caught by a soldier
questions.explain: His spur caught on a flag, and he landed awkwardly after the drop of about twelve feet.

questions.q: Which Latin phrase did many witnesses recall Booth shouting after he shot Lincoln?
questions.explain: The phrase means "thus always to tyrants," though witnesses disagreed about what he exactly said.

questions.q: Which official was attacked in his home by conspirator Lewis Powell on the night of April 14, 1865?
options: Secretary of the Navy Gideon Welles
questions.explain: Powell stabbed Seward in the face and neck, but Seward survived.

questions.q: Which conspirator was assigned to kill Vice President Andrew Johnson but lost his nerve and never made an attempt?
questions.explain: Atzerodt spent the night drinking instead of attacking Johnson at the Kirkwood House.

questions.q: Which conspirator guided Lewis Powell to Seward's house and fled with Booth, surrendering at the Garrett farm?
questions.explain: Herold surrendered on April 26, 1865, after Booth refused to give himself up.

questions.q: Which doctor splinted Booth's broken leg during his escape?
questions.explain: Dr. Samuel Mudd set and splinted Booth's broken leg at his Maryland farm during the escape. He was later convicted as a conspirator and pardoned by Andrew Johnson in 1869.

questions.q: On what date was Booth shot at the Garrett farm in Virginia after refusing to surrender?
questions.explain: The manhunt for Booth ended about twelve days after the shooting.

questions.q: Which Union sergeant shot Booth at the Garrett farm?
questions.explain: Corbett shot Booth after he refused to surrender, while Herold gave himself up.

questions.q: What reward did the government offer for Booth's capture after the assassination?
questions.explain: Smaller rewards of $25,000 each were offered for conspirators Herold and John Surratt.

questions.q: Where was John Surratt, a conspirator who had fled, captured in 1866?
questions.explain: Surratt was the son of Mary Surratt, who was hanged in 1865, and was a suspected conspirator.

questions.q: Which woman was hanged in July 1865 for her role in the conspiracy?
questions.explain: Surratt was among those hanged in July 1865 after a military trial.

questions.q: Who administered the oath of office to Andrew Johnson as president on the morning of April 15, 1865?
questions.explain: Johnson became the seventeenth president hours after Lincoln died.

questions.q: Lincoln's funeral train carried his remains through how many states on its way to Illinois?
questions.explain: The train followed much the same route Lincoln had traveled to Washington in 1861, stopping in major cities.

questions.q: Which famous general and his wife declined an invitation to attend Our American Cousin with the Lincolns?
questions.explain: After the Grants declined, Major Rathbone and Clara Harris went with the Lincolns instead.

questions.q: What was Booth's original plan against Lincoln, which failed on March 17, 1865?
options: To shoot him at his inauguration
questions.explain: Booth turned to assassination after the kidnapping scheme failed and Richmond fell.

questions.q: What did Booth say after hearing Lincoln's last public speech on April 11, 1865?
options: "That is the last speech he will ever make"
"It will be the death of the South"
questions.explain: Booth heard the speech from the crowd outside the White House, where Lincoln spoke of giving some Black men the vote.

questions.q: What was the building that became Ford's Theatre originally used for before John T. Ford leased it in 1861?
questions.explain: The building was built in 1833 as the second meeting house of the First Baptist Church of Washington.

questions.q: What happened to the first Ford's Theatre building in 1862?
options: A flood closed it for two years
The Army seized it as a hospital
A fire destroyed it, and it was rebuilt
questions.explain: A fire destroyed the first Ford's Theatre in December 1862. John T. Ford rebuilt it, and the new theatre opened in August 1863, less than two years before the assassination.

questions.q: After the assassination, what did the government do to Ford's Theatre when John T. Ford planned to reopen it in July 1865?
options: The Secretary of War ordered it closed
Congress closed it by law immediately
Ford sold it to the Baptist church
questions.explain: When Ford tried to reopen it in July 1865, Secretary of War Edwin Stanton had troops seize the theater; the government later bought the building and turned it into offices.

questions.q: How did the federal government use the Ford's Theatre building from 1866 to 1887?
options: As the first home of the Library of Congress
As a War Department office, with the Army Medical Museum on the third floor
questions.explain: After the assassination the government used the building for War Department offices, with the Army Medical Museum on the third floor. In 1893 part of the floors collapsed, killing 22 clerks.

questions.q: What happened to Ford's Theatre on June 9, 1893?
questions.explain: The collapse also injured 68 other workers, and the building was later repaired.

questions.q: When did a Lincoln museum open on the first floor of the old Ford's Theatre building?
questions.explain: The opening on Lincoln's birthday came just before the National Park Service took the building over in 1933.

questions.q: On what date did the restored Ford's Theatre reopen as a working theatre, with a televised celebration led by Helen Hayes?
questions.explain: Congress funded the restoration in 1964, and the theatre reopened 103 years after Lincoln was shot.

questions.q: In what year did Ford's Theatre reopen after an 18-month renovation, timed to the 200th anniversary of Lincoln's birth?
questions.explain: A reopening gala with President Barack Obama was held on February 11, 2009, the eve of the bicentennial of Lincoln's birth.

questions.q: Who sits in the presidential box at Ford's Theatre during performances today?
options: No one; the box is never occupied
questions.explain: The box is furnished with replicas to show how it looked on the night of the assassination, and no one uses it during events.

questions.q: What does the Ford's Theatre Society, which runs the site, operate in addition to theatre programming?
options: The Center for Education and Leadership, which opened in 2012
questions.explain: The center, which opened in 2012, stands across the street from the theatre.

questions.q: Which museum beneath the theatre holds part of a large collection of Lincoln items gathered by Osborn Oldroyd?
questions.explain: Oldroyd, a Civil War veteran, had earlier run a Lincoln museum in the Petersen House.

questions.q: About how many people sat in the audience at Ford's Theatre on the night of the assassination, according to NPS estimates?
questions.explain: The National Park Service says about 1,700, though the number can never be known for certain.

questions.q: Where was Abraham Lincoln born, in a one-room log cabin on February 12, 1809?
questions.explain: He later made his career as a lawyer and politician in Illinois.

questions.q: How many terms did Lincoln serve in the Illinois state legislature before choosing not to run again?
questions.explain: He was first elected in 1834 and won re-election in 1836, 1838 and 1840.

questions.q: In which 1858 speech did Lincoln say that "a house divided against itself cannot stand"?
options: The House Divided speech in Springfield
questions.explain: He delivered it on June 16, 1858, as he accepted the Republican nomination for the U.S. Senate.

questions.q: How many joint debates did Lincoln and Stephen Douglas hold across Illinois in 1858?
questions.explain: Douglas won the state legislature's vote for the Senate seat, 54 to 46.

questions.q: The Homestead Act of 1862, signed by Lincoln, gave a settler how much land after five years of living on it?
questions.explain: A settler could also buy the land for $1.25 an acre after six months.

questions.q: The Morrill Land Grant Act of 1862 gave states federal land to sell to fund what?
options: Colleges teaching agriculture and mechanical arts
questions.explain: The act granted each state 30,000 acres of federal land for each member of Congress, to be sold to fund the colleges.

questions.q: What were "greenbacks," created by the Legal Tender Act of 1862?
options: Silver coins stamped with Lincoln's portrait
Paper money not backed by gold or silver
Bank notes issued by state governments
Treasury bonds sold to foreign investors
questions.explain: Greenbacks were paper money backed only by the government's credit, not by gold or silver. The Union issued them to help pay for the Civil War, and they took their name from their green ink.

questions.q: The Revenue Act of 1861 set the first federal income tax, during the Civil War, at what rate on incomes over $800?
questions.explain: The 1861 tax was replaced by the broader Revenue Act of 1862 before it took effect.

questions.q: Which areas did the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 NOT apply to?
options: Any state west of the Mississippi
Loyal slave states and parts of the Confederacy under Union control
Only the border state of Delaware
questions.explain: The proclamation affected areas still in rebellion, which was a military measure.

questions.q: How many people died in the New York City draft riots of July 1863?
questions.explain: The official toll is usually given as 119 or 120; many victims were Black residents, and federal troops ended the violence.

questions.q: What power did Lincoln use early in the Civil War to hold suspected disloyal people without trial, leading to thousands of arrests?
options: He declared a national state of siege
He invoked the Alien and Sedition Acts
He ordered a presidential pardon system
He suspended the writ of habeas corpus
questions.explain: Lincoln suspended the writ of habeas corpus in parts of the North; Chief Justice Taney objected in Ex parte Merryman.

questions.q: When did the House of Representatives pass the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished slavery?
questions.explain: States ratified the amendment in December 1865, after Lincoln's death.

questions.q: Lincoln was shot just days after which event, which signaled the end of the Civil War in Virginia?
options: Lee's surrender at Appomattox Court House
questions.explain: Lee surrendered on April 9, 1865, and Lincoln was shot on April 14.

questions.q: Which architect designed the Lincoln Memorial as a temple modeled on the Parthenon?
questions.explain: Bacon studied Greek architecture and worked on the memorial from 1914 to 1922.

questions.q: Who carved French's statue of Lincoln from white Georgia marble?
questions.explain: Six brothers in a New York marble workshop carved it in blocks that were fitted together.

questions.q: How many blocks of Georgia marble make up the Lincoln statue?
questions.explain: The seams are nearly invisible after the pieces were fitted together.

questions.q: How tall is the seated statue of Lincoln?
questions.explain: French first planned a statue about 10 feet tall, then enlarged it to fit the huge chamber.

questions.q: How many exterior Doric columns does the Lincoln Memorial have, one for each state in the Union when Lincoln died?
questions.explain: The Lincoln Memorial has 36 exterior Doric columns, one for each state in the Union at Lincoln's death in 1865. The names of those states are carved above the columns.

questions.q: The exterior of the Lincoln Memorial is built of which kind of marble?
questions.explain: Bacon insisted on stone from several states, including Colorado for the walls.

questions.q: Who painted the two interior murals of the Lincoln Memorial, each 60 feet long?
questions.explain: Jules Guerin painted the two large allegorical murals, which sit above the carved texts of the Gettysburg Address and the Second Inaugural Address inside the memorial.

questions.q: The inscription above Lincoln's statue was written by an art critic. What was his name?
questions.explain: Cortissoz wrote that Lincoln's memory is enshrined forever in the temple and in the hearts of the people.

questions.q: Which two Lincoln speeches are carved on the interior walls of the Lincoln Memorial?
options: The First Inaugural Address and the House Divided speech
The Cooper Union address and the Emancipation Proclamation
The Peoria speech and the Lyceum address
The Gettysburg Address and the Second Inaugural Address
questions.explain: Longman carved decorations around the two speeches under French's direction.

questions.q: Which writer described Lincoln as a mix of "steel and velvet"?
questions.explain: Carl Sandburg used the phrase "steel and velvet" for Lincoln in a 1959 speech to Congress. Sandburg wrote a multivolume Lincoln biography and won a Pulitzer Prize for it.

questions.q: Which of Lincoln's children, then aged 78, attended the 1922 dedication?
questions.explain: Robert Todd Lincoln, then 78, attended the 1922 dedication. He was the only one of Abraham and Mary Lincoln's four sons to live to adulthood.

questions.q: How were prominent Black guests treated at the 1922 dedication of the Lincoln Memorial?
options: They were seated in a separate, segregated section
They were seated beside the speakers in the front rows
questions.explain: NPS notes the 1922 crowd was segregated by race, and Robert Moton spoke about discrimination while addressing it.

questions.q: On which date did construction of the Lincoln Memorial begin with a groundbreaking?
questions.explain: Ground was broken for the Lincoln Memorial on February 12, 1914, the 105th anniversary of Lincoln's birth. The finished memorial was dedicated in May 1922.

questions.q: What happened at the Lincoln Memorial on May 9, 1970?
options: The memorial was closed for repairs
President Nixon met briefly with antiwar protesters
questions.explain: In the early morning of May 9, 1970, days after the Kent State shootings, President Nixon made an unplanned visit to the memorial and talked briefly with students protesting the war.

questions.q: In what year was an engraved marker placed on the Lincoln Memorial steps at the spot where King spoke in 1963?
questions.explain: The spot was engraved in 2003, on the 40th anniversary of the March on Washington.

questions.q: Which U.S. paper money has had the Lincoln Memorial on its reverse since 1929?
questions.explain: Lincoln himself appears on the front of the five-dollar bill.

questions.q: The Lincoln Memorial appeared on the reverse of which coin from 1959 to 2008?
questions.explain: The memorial design appeared on the penny's back for nearly fifty years.

questions.q: When was the Lincoln Memorial listed on the National Register of Historic Places?
questions.explain: October 15, 1966, was the day the National Historic Preservation Act became law and created the National Register. Many federal landmarks, including Ford's Theatre, were listed that same day.

questions.q: How tall is each of the Lincoln Memorial's exterior Doric columns?
questions.explain: Each of the 36 exterior Doric columns is 44 feet tall. The memorial as a whole rises about 99 feet above its foundation.

questions.q: What material forms the pedestal under the seated statue of Lincoln in the Lincoln Memorial?
questions.explain: The pedestal under the seated Lincoln is made of Tennessee marble. The statue itself was carved from blocks of white Georgia marble.

questions.q: Which student of Daniel Chester French carved the decorations around the speeches inside the Lincoln Memorial?
questions.explain: Longman was born into poverty and became a leading American sculptor.

questions.q: Which architect designed the Jefferson Memorial, though he died in 1937 before it was built?
questions.explain: Pope's partners Daniel Higgins and Otto Eggers carried the design through construction.

questions.q: Who laid the cornerstone of the Jefferson Memorial on November 15, 1939, burying 15 volumes of Jefferson's publications inside it?
questions.explain: President Franklin D. Roosevelt laid the Jefferson Memorial's cornerstone in 1939. He also dedicated the finished memorial on April 13, 1943, the 200th anniversary of Jefferson's birth.

questions.q: Which sculptor made the bronze statue of Jefferson in the center of the Jefferson Memorial?
questions.explain: The bronze statue is 19 feet tall and shows Jefferson holding the Declaration of Independence in his left hand.

questions.q: Why did the Jefferson Memorial open in 1943 with a plaster statue of Jefferson?
options: The sculptor had died before finishing
Wartime shortages of metal delayed the bronze statue
Congress had not yet approved the final design
questions.explain: World War II shortages of metal delayed the bronze statue, so a painted plaster version stood in the memorial at first. The 19-foot bronze statue was installed in 1947.

questions.q: Which sculptor created the pediment relief of the Jefferson Memorial showing the five-man drafting committee presenting the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: The five members are Jefferson, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, Roger Sherman and Robert Livingston.

questions.q: How many Ionic columns form the circular colonnade of the Jefferson Memorial?
questions.explain: The memorial has an open-air circular colonnade beneath a shallow dome.

questions.q: The Jefferson Memorial's exterior is built of white marble from which state?
questions.explain: The marble is Imperial Danby from Vermont, while the interior walls are white Georgia marble.

questions.q: Which letter of Jefferson's, written to Benjamin Rush on September 23, 1800, provides the quotation around the dome's frieze?
options: The one proclaiming "every generation needs a new revolution"
The one urging "peace, commerce, and honest friendship with all nations"
The one swearing "eternal hostility against every form of tyranny over the mind of man"
questions.explain: NPS lists the line, from the 1800 letter to Rush, among the memorial's inscriptions.

questions.q: Which Jefferson document provides the inscription on the southwest portico of the Jefferson Memorial, beginning "We hold these truths to be self-evident"?
options: The Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom
Notes on the State of Virginia
questions.explain: The inscription excerpts the best-known words of the Declaration.

questions.q: The memorial's inscription "Almighty God hath created the mind free" comes from Jefferson's bill concerning what?
questions.explain: He drafted the bill in 1777, it was introduced in 1779, and it passed in 1786.

questions.q: A memorial inscription taken from an 1816 letter to Samuel Kercheval says Jefferson was not an advocate for what?
options: Frequent changes in laws and constitutions
questions.explain: The passage shows a cautious side of Jefferson on altering the system of government.

questions.q: Japanese cherry trees were planted near the Tidal Basin in 1912. Whose gift were they?
questions.explain: The mayor of Tokyo sent about three thousand trees, which are now a spring attraction in Washington.

questions.q: What happened in November 1938, during the early work on the Jefferson Memorial site, known as the Cherry Tree Rebellion?
options: The Army blew up a seawall
President Roosevelt cut the first tree himself
Women protested the clearing of cherry trees at the site
questions.explain: On November 17, 1938, about 50 women marched on the White House, and the next day some chained themselves to a tree at the site.

questions.q: Which federal arts body objected to the Pantheon-style design of the Jefferson Memorial before President Roosevelt overrode it?
questions.explain: The memorial commission appealed to Roosevelt, who overrode the Commission of Fine Arts and ordered construction to begin.

questions.q: Which landscape architect designed the grounds around the Jefferson Memorial?
questions.explain: Olmsted, appointed landscape architect in 1938, planned the grounds around the memorial.

questions.q: Where was Thomas Jefferson born on April 13, 1743?
questions.explain: Jefferson was born at Shadwell, his father's plantation in Goochland County, Virginia; the area became part of Albemarle County in 1744. He later built Monticello on a nearby mountain.

questions.q: Jefferson studied law under which Virginia teacher from 1762 to 1767?
questions.explain: Jefferson read law under George Wythe, one of Virginia's leading lawyers and later a signer of the Declaration. Jefferson was admitted to the Virginia bar in 1767.

questions.q: How long did Jefferson spend writing the Declaration of Independence in June 1776?
options: About two and a half weeks, from June 11 to June 28
questions.explain: Jefferson drafted the Declaration in about two and a half weeks in June 1776 for the Committee of Five. Congress revised his draft and approved it on July 4, 1776.

questions.q: Which man was NOT one of the five members of the Committee of Five that drafted the Declaration of Independence?
questions.explain: The committee also included Benjamin Franklin and Jefferson.

questions.q: Jefferson served as governor of Virginia from June 1779 to when?
questions.explain: He served two years as governor during the Revolutionary War.

questions.q: In which city did Jefferson have 200 copies of his Notes on the State of Virginia privately printed in 1785?
questions.explain: A French translation followed, and John Stockdale issued the first public English edition in London in 1787.

questions.q: In 1785, Jefferson was appointed to represent the United States as minister to which country?
questions.explain: Congress named Jefferson minister to France in 1785, succeeding Benjamin Franklin. He served in Paris until September 1789, then returned home and became secretary of state in March 1790.

questions.q: Which post did Jefferson hold under President George Washington, beginning in 1790?
questions.explain: Jefferson became the first secretary of state in 1790, serving in Washington's first Cabinet until the end of 1793. He often clashed there with Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton.

questions.q: For how many years did Jefferson serve as president, from 1801 to 1809?
questions.explain: Jefferson served two full four-year terms, from 1801 to 1809, for eight years in all. He followed John Adams and was succeeded by James Madison.

questions.q: What date does the Louisiana Purchase treaty bear?
questions.explain: The Louisiana Purchase treaty, negotiated in Paris by Robert Livingston and James Monroe, is dated April 30, 1803 (it was formally signed a few days later). The United States paid about $15 million for the territory.

questions.q: Which two American negotiators were first authorized to spend up to $10 million for New Orleans and the Floridas?
questions.explain: When Napoleon offered all of Louisiana, they agreed to $15 million.

questions.q: What concern did Jefferson, a strict constructionist, have about the Louisiana Purchase?
options: He thought the price was too low for such land
He worried Britain would block the sale
He doubted that the Constitution gave the president power to acquire new territory
He wanted Spain to receive a share
questions.explain: His wish to expand across the continent outweighed his doubts.

questions.q: Which 1803 Supreme Court decision, written by Chief Justice John Marshall, established judicial review?
questions.explain: The Court refused William Marbury's request but ruled that part of the Judiciary Act of 1789 was unconstitutional.

questions.q: What did the Embargo Act of 1807 do?
options: Raised tariffs on British goods only
Halted American exports to foreign countries
questions.explain: The Embargo Act of 1807 barred American ships from sailing to foreign ports, halting exports. Jefferson hoped to pressure Britain and France, but the law hurt American trade and was repealed in 1809.

questions.q: After the British burned the Library of Congress during the War of 1812, what did Jefferson do with his personal library?
options: He sold it to the U.S. government to replace the lost Library of Congress
He donated it to the University of Virginia
He burned it to prevent capture
He gave it to Monticello's staff
questions.explain: Congress paid $23,950 for his library of 6,487 volumes in 1815.

questions.q: On what date did Jefferson die at Monticello, at age 83?
questions.explain: He died fifty years to the day after the Declaration was adopted.

questions.q: Robert Mills's original design for the Washington Monument had what feature that was never built?
options: A statue of Washington on a horse atop the obelisk
A circular colonnade at the base
questions.explain: In April 1848 the society directed Mills to build the obelisk first, deferring the colonnaded "pantheon," which was never built.

questions.q: On what date was the cornerstone of the Washington Monument laid?
questions.explain: President James K. Polk and Congressman Abraham Lincoln were among those at the cornerstone ceremony.

questions.q: About how high had the Washington Monument risen when donations ran out and work stopped in 1854?
questions.explain: Work stalled for more than two decades, partly because of the Civil War.

questions.q: A political group gained control of the Washington Monument society in the 1850s, and the masonry it added was later removed for poor quality. What was the group?
questions.explain: The Know-Nothings added poor-quality masonry that was later removed, and work stalled until Congress took over construction in 1876.

questions.q: Which Army Corps of Engineers officer completed the Washington Monument after Congress took over in 1876?
questions.explain: Casey was appointed engineer in charge in 1878 and strengthened the foundation before building upward.

questions.q: What metal was used for the tip of the Washington Monument, set in place on December 6, 1884?
questions.explain: The 9-inch cast aluminum pyramid was set on December 6, 1884; aluminum was still a rare, costly metal.

questions.q: On what date was the completed Washington Monument dedicated?
questions.explain: The finished Washington Monument was dedicated on February 21, 1885, with President Chester A. Arthur attending. Its capstone had been set in December 1884.

questions.q: On what date did the Washington Monument officially open to the public with a passenger elevator?
questions.explain: The monument officially opened to the public on October 9

questions.q: For about how many years was the Washington Monument the tallest structure in the world, from 1884 until another landmark opened in 1889?
questions.explain: Finished in 1884, the Washington Monument was the world's tallest structure for about five years, until the Eiffel Tower in Paris surpassed it in 1889.

questions.q: What was the total cost of building the Washington Monument from 1848 to 1888?
questions.explain: The Washington Monument cost about $1.2 million to build; the National Park Service gives the total as $1,187,710. Construction stalled for years before the government finished it.

questions.q: How tall is the Washington Monument?
questions.explain: The marble obelisk, finished in 1884, has long been listed at 555 feet, 5 1/8 inches tall on a base about 55 feet square; a 2014 survey measured 554 feet, 7 11/32 inches.

questions.q: How many commemorative stones donated by states, cities and groups are set in the Washington Monument's interior walls, according to NPS?
questions.explain: The stones come from individuals, groups, cities, states and countries.

questions.q: After earthquake repairs costing about $15 million, when did the Washington Monument reopen to visitors?
questions.explain: Billionaire David Rubenstein matched $7.5 million of federal funding for repairs.

questions.q: Which businessman matched $7.5 million in federal money to help pay for repairs after the 2011 earthquake?
questions.explain: The repairs cost $15 million in all and took nearly three years.

questions.q: What happened at the Washington Monument in December 1982?
options: A man threatened to blow it up in a ten-hour standoff
A fire broke out in the elevator
questions.explain: Norman Mayer claimed his van held explosives; police shot him as he tried to drive away, and the van held none.

questions.q: In which year was the Washington National Monument Society formed to build the memorial?
questions.explain: The Washington National Monument Society was formed in 1833 to raise private money for a memorial to Washington. Construction on the monument did not begin until 1848.

questions.q: On what date was George Washington born in Virginia?
questions.explain: He was born at Popes Creek in Westmoreland County, Virginia.

questions.q: In July 1754, Washington surrendered which fort to a French force, an early event in the French and Indian War?
questions.explain: Washington, then a 22-year-old colonel commanding the Virginia Regiment, surrendered Fort Necessity to the French on July 3, 1754. The clash helped start the French and Indian War.

questions.q: Washington served in 1755 as an aide to which British general, who was killed at the Battle of the Monongahela?
questions.explain: Washington was an aide to General Edward Braddock, who was mortally wounded when French and Native forces routed his army at the Monongahela in July 1755.

questions.q: On what date did Washington marry Martha Dandridge Custis?
questions.explain: Washington married Martha Dandridge Custis on January 6, 1759. She was the wealthy widow of Daniel Parke Custis and brought two young children to the marriage.

questions.q: What did the Second Continental Congress do on June 15, 1775, in selecting Washington?
options: Elected him commander of the Continental Army
Selected him to write the Constitution
questions.explain: On June 15, 1775, the Second Continental Congress elected Washington commander in chief of the Continental Army, which it had created the day before.

questions.q: British forces evacuated Boston on March 17, 1776, after Washington's troops fortified which place?
questions.explain: The British left Boston after the fortification of the heights.

questions.q: Which 1781 victory, with French help, essentially won American independence?
questions.explain: The French navy's victory in the Battle of the Chesapeake had cut off Cornwallis's escape by water.

questions.q: Which role did Washington hold at the 1787 Constitutional Convention?
options: Chair of the Committee of Style
Leader of the Virginia delegation's opposition
questions.explain: Delegates elected him once a quorum had been reached on May 25.

questions.q: How was Washington elected president in 1789 and again in 1792?
options: By the House of Representatives after a tie
With a narrow margin over John Adams
questions.explain: Washington received a vote from every elector who cast a ballot in both 1789 and 1792. He is the only president to win a unanimous Electoral College vote.

questions.q: Where did Washington take the oath of office as president on April 30, 1789?
questions.explain: Washington took the first presidential oath at Federal Hall in New York City, which was then the nation's capital. The capital moved to Philadelphia in 1790.

questions.q: Who served as Washington's first Secretary of the Treasury, proposing that the federal government assume state war debts?
questions.explain: Hamilton also proposed full repayment of bonds and a national bank.

questions.q: On what date did Washington sign the bill creating the First Bank of the United States?
questions.explain: Hamilton's opinion persuaded Washington despite Jefferson's objections.

questions.q: In 1794 Washington summoned the militias of four states in response to what uprising?
questions.explain: Washington personally joined the militia force for part of the march west.

questions.q: In his Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796, what did Washington announce?
options: That he would lead the Army again
That he would not seek another term
That he would resign as general
That he would form a party
questions.explain: The Farewell Address announced that Washington would not seek a third term. It also warned Americans against political parties and permanent foreign alliances.

questions.q: On what date did Washington die at Mount Vernon at age 67?
questions.explain: His will provided for the eventual freeing of the people he held in slavery.

questions.q: What did Washington's will provide regarding the enslaved people at Mount Vernon?
options: Their sale to pay his debts
Their transfer to Martha's family permanently
questions.explain: His will freed the people he owned after Martha's death; the Custis family held others, who were not freed.

questions.q: Washington's neutrality policy was issued during which foreign conflict?
questions.explain: Washington issued his Neutrality Proclamation in 1793, after revolutionary France went to war with Britain and other European powers. He wanted to keep the young nation out of the conflict.

questions.q: How many outdoor "rooms" does the Franklin D. Roosevelt Memorial have, one for each of his terms?
questions.explain: Each room is marked by quotations from his speeches and has water features.

questions.q: Which landscape architect was selected in 1974 to design the Franklin D. Roosevelt Memorial?
questions.explain: Halprin's design opened in 1997 as a series of four outdoor rooms.

questions.q: On what date was the Franklin D. Roosevelt Memorial dedicated by President Bill Clinton?
questions.explain: The dedication came decades after Congress set up the memorial commission in 1955.

questions.q: When did Congress establish the commission that began planning a memorial to Roosevelt?
questions.explain: Congress set up the commission in 1955, but Halprin was not chosen until 1974.

questions.q: The FDR Memorial is distinctive among presidential memorials in Washington for including a statue of whom?
questions.explain: It is the only presidential memorial that depicts a First Lady.

questions.q: What controversy led to the addition of a new statue at the FDR Memorial in January 2001?
options: Critics said the memorial lacked any statue of Churchill
Critics wanted a bigger statue of Eleanor
Critics said the memorial did not show that Roosevelt used a wheelchair
questions.explain: Disability advocates campaigned for the statue, which was unveiled in January 2001.

questions.q: Which animal appears with FDR in sculptures at the Franklin D. Roosevelt Memorial?
questions.explain: The FDR Memorial includes a sculpture of Roosevelt seated with his Scottish terrier, Fala, beside him. Fala was Roosevelt's constant companion during his presidency.

questions.q: A quotation at the memorial comes from Roosevelt's 1936 "I Hate War" speech in which New York town?
questions.explain: Roosevelt gave his "I Hate War" speech at Chautauqua, New York, in August 1936, and a quotation from it is carved at the memorial. In it he described the horrors of war he had seen.

questions.q: What accessibility feature drew criticism when it was installed at the FDR Memorial?
options: Braille that was oversized, poorly spaced and mounted too high to read
A ramp too steep for wheelchairs
Audio guides in only one language
questions.explain: Advocates said the tactile reliefs failed visitors who are blind; a 2021 review found the Braille ranged from hard to read to unrecognizable.

questions.q: About how large is the FDR Memorial, which sits beside the Tidal Basin?
questions.explain: The FDR Memorial covers about 7.5 acres beside the Tidal Basin. It is laid out as four outdoor rooms, one for each of Roosevelt's terms.

questions.q: What did Roosevelt establish in Warm Springs, Georgia, in 1926?
options: A rehabilitation center for polio patients
questions.explain: In 1938 he organized the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis.

questions.q: By what margin did Roosevelt win the governorship of New York in 1928?
questions.explain: Roosevelt won the 1928 race for governor of New York by less than one percentage point, about 26,000 votes out of more than 4 million cast. The narrow win put him on the path to the White House.

questions.q: Roosevelt ran for vice president in 1920 on a ticket with which presidential candidate?
questions.explain: In 1920 Roosevelt was the Democratic nominee for vice president on a ticket headed by Ohio governor James M. Cox. They lost in a landslide to Warren Harding.

questions.q: What did Roosevelt say in his March 4, 1933, inaugural address about fear?
options: "Fear is the mother of all progress"
"Fear and want must both be abolished"
"The only thing we have to fear is fear itself"
questions.explain: In his first inaugural address in 1933, Roosevelt said "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself." He was speaking to a nation in the depths of the Great Depression.

questions.q: What did Roosevelt do on March 6, 1933, two days after taking office?
options: Took the United States off the gold standard permanently
questions.explain: The holiday halted a run on banks and prepared for emergency legislation.

questions.q: What were Roosevelt's "fireside chats"?
options: Radio addresses explaining his policies to the public
questions.explain: Fireside chats were Roosevelt's radio talks explaining his policies directly to Americans. The first, on March 12, 1933, explained his plan to reopen the banks.

questions.q: Over its life from 1933 to 1942, about how many young men served in the Civilian Conservation Corps?
questions.explain: The corps was one of the first New Deal programs, launched in 1933, and nearly 3 million men served.

questions.q: The period from March to June 1933, when Congress passed a burst of Depression-fighting laws, was known as what?
questions.explain: The Hundred Days was the burst of New Deal laws passed from March to June 1933, early in Roosevelt's first term. The laws tackled banks, farming, industry and relief.

questions.q: In which year did Roosevelt sign the Social Security Act, creating old-age insurance and unemployment programs?
questions.explain: The act also gave grants for aid to dependent children and the blind.

questions.q: Which workers did the original Social Security Act exclude from old-age coverage?
questions.explain: Government workers and some nonprofit workers were excluded too.

questions.q: Which Supreme Court decision in May 1935 struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act?
options: Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States
questions.explain: In Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, the "sick chicken" case, the Court unanimously struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act in May 1935.

questions.q: What was Roosevelt's 1937 "court-packing" plan?
options: To reduce the Court to six members
To make the justices elected officials
To add a justice for each sitting justice over age 70
To require the Court to approve all laws in advance
questions.explain: Roosevelt proposed adding a justice for each sitting justice over 70, up to six new seats, to win rulings for the New Deal. The plan failed in the Senate in July 1937.

questions.q: A sharp recession began in 1937. By about how much did industrial production fall?
questions.explain: The Federal Reserve's history says industrial production fell 32 percent, and unemployment rose sharply again.

questions.q: What was the Lend-Lease program, enacted in March 1941?
options: It leased American warships to Japan
It kept arms and supplies flowing to Britain and other Allies
It sold land to the Allies
It loaned money to the Axis powers
questions.explain: The first appropriation was $7 billion, and the total grew to more than $50 billion.

questions.q: What agreement did Roosevelt and Winston Churchill issue in August 1941 to state their war goals?
questions.explain: The statement preceded the United States' entry into the war.

questions.q: Which four freedoms did Roosevelt name in his January 6, 1941, address?
options: Speech, worship, freedom from want and freedom from fear
questions.explain: In his 1941 State of the Union address, Roosevelt named freedom of speech, freedom of worship, freedom from want and freedom from fear as goals for the postwar world.

questions.q: Which artist painted a series illustrating the four freedoms that toured the country in a war bond drive?
questions.explain: The Saturday Evening Post published the paintings after the government had at first declined his offer.

questions.q: At which November 1943 conference did Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agree on a 1944 invasion of France?
questions.explain: At the Tehran Conference in November 1943, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin agreed on an Allied invasion of France in 1944. It came on D-Day, June 6, 1944.

questions.q: At the January 1943 Casablanca Conference, the Allies agreed to invade which island after clearing North Africa?
questions.explain: The invasion of Sicily began in July 1943 and opened the way to the Italian mainland.

questions.q: Which amendment, ratified in 1951, limited presidents to two terms?
questions.explain: The Twenty-second Amendment, ratified in 1951, limits presidents to two elected terms. It followed Roosevelt's four election victories, from 1932 to 1944.

questions.q: Which vice president served with Roosevelt from 1933 to 1941?
questions.explain: John Nance Garner of Texas was Roosevelt's vice president for his first two terms, 1933 to 1941. Henry Wallace served next, and Harry Truman served in 1945.

questions.q: At what age did Roosevelt begin attending Groton School?
questions.explain: Roosevelt entered Groton School in Massachusetts in 1896, at age 14, after being taught at home by tutors. He went on to Harvard in 1900.

questions.q: On what date in 1905 did Franklin marry Eleanor Roosevelt?
questions.explain: Franklin married Eleanor Roosevelt, a distant cousin, on March 17, 1905. Her uncle, President Theodore Roosevelt, gave the bride away.

questions.q: What was Franklin Roosevelt's distinction regarding presidential terms?
options: He was the first to serve two terms
He is the only president elected more than twice
questions.explain: Roosevelt is the only president elected more than twice: he won in 1932, 1936, 1940 and 1944. He died in April 1945, early in his fourth term.

questions.q: On December 7, 1941, which naval base did Japan attack?
questions.explain: Japan attacked the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941, killing more than 2,400 Americans. Congress declared war on Japan the next day.

questions.q: In what state was Frederick Douglass born into slavery around 1818?
questions.explain: He was born Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey at Holme Hill Farm in Talbot County, Maryland.
