questions.q: What was Frederick Douglass's birth name?
questions.explain: He took the name Douglass after reaching New Bedford, Massachusetts, in 1838.

questions.q: Who began teaching young Frederick to read in Baltimore in 1827?
questions.explain: Sophia Auld, wife of Hugh Auld, began teaching young Frederick the alphabet in Baltimore. Her husband stopped the lessons, but Douglass kept learning on his own.

questions.q: After Douglass fought back in August 1834, which brutal slave breaker did not whip him again?
questions.explain: Douglass fought Covey in August 1834 and was not whipped again.

questions.q: On what date did Douglass escape slavery by train and boat?
questions.explain: He reached New York City and married Anna Murray on September 15.

questions.q: To which Massachusetts city did Douglass and Anna Murray move in 1838, where he took the name Douglass?
questions.explain: He worked there and soon met abolitionists, including William Lloyd Garrison.

questions.q: In 1841 Douglass was hired as a lecturer by which organization?
questions.explain: He had spoken at an anti-slavery meeting in Nantucket that August.

questions.q: What was the title of Douglass's first autobiography, published in May 1845?
options: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass
Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave
questions.explain: The Narrative revealed his identity and put him at risk of recapture.

questions.q: Why did Douglass sail to Britain in August 1845?
options: Partly to avoid recapture after his Narrative revealed his identity
To negotiate for the Union Army
questions.explain: Douglass's 1845 Narrative named his former owner, so he risked recapture as a fugitive. He sailed to Britain that August and lectured in Britain and Ireland until spring 1847, nearly two years.

questions.q: How was Douglass's legal freedom obtained in December 1846?
options: He was pardoned by the governor of Maryland
British supporters raised money to buy it
questions.explain: British supporters raised about 150 pounds to buy Douglass's freedom from his owner in 1846. His manumission papers were filed in Baltimore, making him legally free.

questions.q: Douglass attended which July 1848 convention, afterward supporting votes for women?
options: The Seneca Falls Women's Rights Convention
The Free Soil Convention at Buffalo
questions.explain: Douglass attended the 1848 Seneca Falls Women's Rights Convention and spoke in favor of the resolution calling for women's right to vote.

questions.q: Which July 5, 1852, speech by Douglass asked what the Fourth of July meant to the enslaved?
options: "The Meaning of July Fourth for the Negro"
"What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?"
questions.explain: Douglass gave "What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?" in Rochester, New York, on July 5, 1852. He contrasted the nation's celebration of liberty with the reality of slavery.

questions.q: In which year did Douglass publish My Bondage and My Freedom, his second autobiography?
questions.explain: He published it in August 1855, ten years after the Narrative.

questions.q: Which abolitionist did Douglass meet in 1859, declining to join his planned raid on Harpers Ferry?
questions.explain: Douglass fled to Canada and England after the raid, fearing arrest.

questions.q: Which Massachusetts regiment included two of Douglass's sons, Lewis and Charles?
questions.explain: Lewis and Charles Douglass enlisted in the 54th Massachusetts, one of the first Black regiments in the Union Army. Their father helped recruit Black soldiers for it in 1863.

questions.q: Douglass met President Lincoln in August 1863 to protest what?
options: The slow pace of westward expansion
questions.explain: He pressed for equal treatment, including equal pay and protection.

questions.q: In March 1865, Douglass attended which event with Lincoln?
options: The signing of the Thirteenth Amendment
questions.explain: Douglass attended Lincoln's second inauguration in March 1865. At the White House reception afterward, Lincoln greeted him warmly and asked his opinion of the address.

questions.q: In 1870, Douglass celebrated the ratification of which amendment?
questions.explain: It said the right to vote could not be denied because of race.

questions.q: In 1872, a fire at Douglass's home in Rochester led him to move to where?
questions.explain: After a fire destroyed his Rochester home in 1872, Douglass moved to Washington, D.C. He later bought Cedar Hill in Anacostia and lived there until his death in 1895.

questions.q: In 1874 Frederick Douglass became president of which bank, whose collapse cost him heavy personal losses?
options: The Bank of the United States
questions.explain: Douglass became president of the Freedman's Savings Bank in 1874, shortly before it failed. He had put his own money into it, and thousands of Black depositors lost savings.

questions.q: In 1877 Douglass was appointed to which post in the District of Columbia?
questions.explain: President Rutherford B. Hayes appointed Douglass U.S. Marshal for the District of Columbia in 1877. In 1881 he became the District's Recorder of Deeds.

questions.q: What post did Douglass take in 1889?
options: Minister Resident and Consul General to Haiti
questions.explain: President Benjamin Harrison named Douglass Minister Resident and Consul General to Haiti in 1889. He served in the post until 1891.

questions.q: Which book did Douglass publish in 1881, reflecting on his career?
options: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass
questions.explain: He published it as a third autobiography, in the year he became Recorder of Deeds.

questions.q: Whom did Douglass marry in 1884, two years after the death of his first wife?
questions.explain: Douglass married Helen Pitts in 1884. His first wife, Anna Murray Douglass, to whom he had been married for 44 years, had died in August 1882.

questions.q: What did Douglass condemn in his last major address, "Lessons of the Hour," in January 1894?
questions.explain: In "Lessons of the Hour," given in January 1894, about a year before his death, Douglass condemned lynching and the false charges used to justify it.

questions.q: On what date did Frederick Douglass die at Cedar Hill?
questions.explain: He was buried in Mount Hope Cemetery in Rochester, New York.

questions.q: Where was Frederick Douglass buried?
options: Mount Hope Cemetery, Rochester, New York
questions.explain: Rochester had been his home from 1847 until a fire destroyed his house in 1872.

questions.q: How much did Douglass pay for the Cedar Hill house and about nine acres?
questions.explain: NPS says he paid $6,700 to the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company in 1877.

questions.q: What notable restriction was on the original deed of Cedar Hill, which Douglass broke?
options: A rule against selling to Union veterans
questions.explain: He was one of the first Black men in Washington to break such a covenant.

questions.q: Douglass expanded Cedar Hill from 14 rooms to how many?
questions.explain: He also enlarged the property to about 15 acres and added a library.

questions.q: What portraits hung in Douglass's library at Cedar Hill?
options: George Washington, Thomas Jefferson and Andrew Jackson
Harriet Tubman, Sojourner Truth and Booker T. Washington
Abraham Lincoln, Ulysses Grant and Frederick Law Olmsted
John Brown, Susan B. Anthony and William Lloyd Garrison
questions.explain: Douglass's library at Cedar Hill held portraits of allies in the fights against slavery and for equal rights, including John Brown, Susan B. Anthony and William Lloyd Garrison.

questions.q: Congress chartered which group on June 6, 1900, for the sole purpose of preserving the Douglass home?
options: The Frederick Douglass Memorial and Historical Association
questions.explain: The association took over the house after Helen Douglass died in 1903.

questions.q: Which national women's organization partnered with the Douglass memorial association in 1916 to pay off the loan and restore Frederick Douglass's house?
options: The Daughters of the American Revolution
The National Association of Colored Women's Clubs
questions.explain: The National Association of Colored Women's Clubs, led in this campaign by Mary B. Talbert, helped pay off the house's debt and restore it. A ceremony marked the restoration in 1922.

questions.q: On September 5, 1962, President Kennedy signed a law transferring Cedar Hill to which agency?
questions.explain: The service restored the house over about ten years and opened it in 1972.

questions.q: In what year did the National Park Service open the restored Douglass home to the public?
questions.explain: The National Park Service opened the restored Cedar Hill to the public in 1972. Congress had made the house part of the national park system in 1962.

questions.q: Which gift is on display at Cedar Hill, among objects from the Douglass family?
options: Abraham Lincoln's cane, sent by Mary Todd Lincoln after his death
A gift from Ulysses Grant's cabinet
questions.explain: Cedar Hill displays gifts tied to Abraham Lincoln and Harriet Beecher Stowe among the Douglass family's objects. The house is furnished much as it was during Douglass's lifetime.

questions.q: Douglass broke with William Lloyd Garrison in May 1851 over what?
questions.explain: Garrison opposed taking part in politics, but Douglass came to favor political action.

questions.q: In September 1841, Douglass was removed from a train for refusing to sit where?
questions.explain: The incident came a month after he began working as a lecturer.

questions.q: In 1871 Douglass served on a commission investigating the annexation of which Caribbean territory?
questions.explain: President Grant sent a commission in 1871 to study annexing Santo Domingo, now the Dominican Republic, and Douglass served with it. The Senate never approved annexation.

questions.q: In 1872 the Equal Rights Party nominated Douglass for vice president without his consent. Whom did he campaign for?
questions.explain: Douglass ignored the Equal Rights Party nomination and campaigned for Republican Ulysses S. Grant, who won reelection in 1872.

questions.q: In 1886 and 1887, Douglass traveled through Europe and which other two countries?
questions.explain: In 1886 and 1887 Douglass and his wife, Helen, toured Europe and also traveled to Egypt and Greece.

questions.q: Which religious denomination does Washington National Cathedral belong to?
questions.explain: Its official name is the Cathedral Church of Saint Peter and Saint Paul.

questions.q: Congress granted a charter for Washington National Cathedral on January 6 of which year?
questions.explain: The charter dedicated it to religion, education and charity.

questions.q: Which Bishop of Washington selected Washington National Cathedral's hilltop site?
questions.explain: Henry Y. Satterlee, the first Bishop of Washington, chose the hilltop site on Mount Saint Alban. He died in 1908, soon after construction began.

questions.q: Which president helped lay the foundation stone of Washington National Cathedral on September 29, 1907?
questions.explain: President Theodore Roosevelt spoke at the laying of the foundation stone on September 29, 1907. The stone includes a piece of rock from a field near Bethlehem.

questions.q: Which president attended the completion of Washington National Cathedral in September 1990, 83 years after construction began?
questions.explain: President George H. W. Bush attended as the final finial was set in September 1990, 83 years after the foundation stone was laid in 1907.

questions.q: How has Washington National Cathedral been funded?
options: By a tax on the Episcopal diocese
By private donors, with no direct federal support
questions.explain: The cathedral says it receives no direct federal government or national church support.

questions.q: Which English architect was the original designer of Washington National Cathedral, dying the same year ground was broken?
questions.explain: Henry Vaughan revised his design, and Frohman completed the building.

questions.q: Which architect, working with the firm Frohman, Robb and Little, served as Washington National Cathedral's principal architect for most of its construction?
questions.explain: Philip Hubert Frohman was the cathedral's principal architect for decades, working with Frohman, Robb and Little. He died in 1972, before the building was finished.

questions.q: Who contributed the landscape plan for the grounds of Washington National Cathedral?
questions.explain: Olmsted Jr. drew up the landscape plan for the cathedral grounds from 1907 into the 1920s; the grounds cover about 57 to 59 acres.

questions.q: How tall is the Gloria in Excelsis Tower, Washington National Cathedral's central tower?
questions.explain: The tower rises 301 feet and stands 676 feet above sea level.

questions.q: How many bells are in Washington National Cathedral's carillon?
questions.explain: The cathedral also has a ring of ten bells for change ringing.

questions.q: Washington National Cathedral's Space Window honors what event and contains a piece of lunar rock?
questions.explain: The Space Window honors the Apollo 11 Moon landing and holds a small piece of lunar rock. It was dedicated on July 21, 1974, the fifth anniversary of the landing.

questions.q: Which sermon did Martin Luther King Jr. give from Washington National Cathedral's Canterbury Pulpit on March 31, 1968?
options: His I Have a Dream speech
questions.explain: On March 31, 1968, King preached his last Sunday sermon from the cathedral's Canterbury Pulpit. He was assassinated in Memphis four days later.

questions.q: Which president is buried in the cathedral, the only president buried in Washington, D.C.?
questions.explain: Woodrow Wilson is buried in Washington National Cathedral, the only president buried in the capital. His burial service was held in Bethlehem Chapel in 1924.

questions.q: Which blind and deaf author is buried in Washington National Cathedral along with her teacher, Anne Sullivan?
questions.explain: Keller's ashes were interred beside Sullivan's at the cathedral in 1968.

questions.q: Which Spanish-American War naval hero is interred in Washington National Cathedral?
questions.explain: Admiral George Dewey, who won the Battle of Manila Bay in 1898, is interred in the cathedral. Others buried there include Cordell Hull and Frank Kellogg.

questions.q: Which presidents have had state funerals at Washington National Cathedral since 2004?
options: Ronald Reagan, Gerald Ford, George H. W. Bush and Jimmy Carter
Franklin Roosevelt and John F. Kennedy
questions.explain: The cathedral has hosted state funerals for five presidents in all.

questions.q: Which feature, sculpted by Jay Hall Carpenter, was chosen in a public design competition for Washington National Cathedral's northwest tower?
options: A bust of Martin Luther King Jr.
questions.explain: The carved head of the film villain became one of the cathedral's best-known features.

questions.q: Who became the first woman to serve as Bishop of Washington, installed in November 2011?
questions.explain: Mariann Budde was installed in November 2011 as the ninth Bishop of Washington and the first woman to hold the post.

questions.q: Who was the first African American Bishop of Washington?
questions.explain: John T. Walker became the first African American Bishop of Washington in 1977. He was the sixth bishop of the diocese.

questions.q: Pierre L'Enfant's original plan for the capital called for what kind of building?
options: A great church for national purposes
questions.explain: The idea of a national church eventually led to the cathedral.

questions.q: After Washington National Cathedral's 2011 earthquake damage, about how much did officials estimate the damage to cost?
questions.explain: The August 2011 Virginia earthquake damaged the cathedral's towers and stonework, and officials estimated repairs at about $25 million. The work took years to complete.

questions.q: What happened to the Lee and Jackson stained-glass windows at Washington National Cathedral in 2017?
questions.explain: The cathedral took down the windows in 2017, and new "Now and Forever" windows were dedicated in 2023.

questions.q: Which famous architect's firm designed Washington's Union Station in the Beaux-Arts style?
questions.explain: Burnham's firm, D. H. Burnham and Company, designed the station in the Beaux-Arts style.

questions.q: Which two railroads built Washington's Union Station?
options: The New York Central and the Erie
The Union Pacific and the Central Pacific
The Pennsylvania Railroad and the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad
The Southern and the Atlantic Coast Line
questions.explain: The Pennsylvania Railroad and the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad jointly built Union Station, which let them close separate stations and clear tracks off the National Mall.

questions.q: Which body passed the 1903 act authorizing construction of Washington's Union Station?
questions.explain: Theodore Roosevelt signed the authorizing act on February 28, 1903.

questions.q: On what date did the first B&O train arrive at Union Station, marking its opening?
questions.explain: Union Station, designed by Daniel Burnham, opened when the first B&O train arrived on October 27, 1907. It replaced two older railroad stations in the city.

questions.q: Union Station's construction wiped out much of which Washington neighborhood?
questions.explain: More than ten blocks of homes were demolished, and Tiber Creek was put into a tunnel.

questions.q: Union Station's design drew on which ancient Roman monuments?
options: The Arch of Constantine and the Baths of Diocletian
The Appian Way and the Circus Maximus
questions.explain: Daniel Burnham modeled Union Station's entrance on the Arch of Constantine and its great main hall on the Baths of Diocletian, both in Rome.

questions.q: How high is the ceiling of the main waiting room at Union Station?
questions.explain: The barrel-vaulted ceiling of Union Station's main waiting room rises 96 feet and is decorated with gold leaf, restored in the 1980s.

questions.q: The 46 Roman legionnaire statues at Union Station are said to represent what?
options: One for each state at the time of opening
One for each of Washington's wards
One for each railroad serving the station
One for each president to that date
questions.explain: The 1907 count matched the 46 states; shields were added after complaints about their nudity.

questions.q: What happened at Union Station on January 15, 1953?
options: A fire gutted the main hall
A bomb exploded in the baggage room
A track collapse injured fifty people
A runaway locomotive crashed into the station, with no one killed
questions.explain: The crash was later echoed in the finale of the 1976 film Silver Streak.

questions.q: On what date did Amtrak take over intercity passenger rail service, including at Union Station?
questions.explain: Amtrak began running most U.S. intercity passenger trains on May 1, 1971, after railroads had struggled for years to keep passenger service going.

questions.q: When did the National Visitor Center at Union Station open, during the Bicentennial?
questions.explain: The center attracted few visitors and closed after a few years.

questions.q: Why was most of Union Station closed in 1981?
options: A railroad strike had closed the tracks
Rain-damaged ceiling pieces fell into the main hall, making it unsafe
questions.explain: The building had been deteriorating since the National Visitor Center failed.

questions.q: Which president signed the Union Station Redevelopment Act on December 29, 1981?
questions.explain: The law paved the way for a private-public restoration of the station.

questions.q: When did the restored Union Station reopen with a new marketplace of shops and restaurants?
questions.explain: After years of decay and a failed visitor center for the 1976 Bicentennial, the restored Union Station reopened on September 29, 1988, with shops and restaurants.

questions.q: Washington's Union Station is the second-busiest station for which railroad's passenger service?
questions.explain: It also connects to the Metro Red Line, MARC and Virginia Railway Express.

questions.q: In 2024 a federal judge ruled that Amtrak could take control of the Union Station operator's lease by what legal process?
questions.explain: Amtrak filed its condemnation claim in 2022, and the case ended in a settlement in March 2025.

questions.q: On what date did the National Air and Space Museum building on the National Mall open?
questions.explain: The National Air and Space Museum's building on the Mall opened on July 1, 1976, timed for the U.S. Bicentennial. It quickly became one of the most visited museums in the world.

questions.q: Which year did Congress create the National Air Museum, the predecessor of today's museum?
questions.explain: Congress created the National Air Museum in 1946, and President Harry Truman signed the act on August 12. It was renamed the National Air and Space Museum in 1966.

questions.q: Which firm's architect Gyo Obata designed the National Air and Space Museum building?
questions.explain: Gyo Obata of the firm HOK designed the museum building, which opened in 1976. Its simple blocks are clad in pink Tennessee marble to match the National Gallery of Art across the Mall.

questions.q: Which Apollo 11 astronaut served as director of the National Air and Space Museum when it opened in 1976?
questions.explain: Collins piloted the command module Columbia, now in the museum.

questions.q: Where is the National Air and Space Museum's annex, the Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center, located?
options: Near Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland
Near Dulles International Airport in Virginia
questions.explain: The Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center stands near Dulles International Airport in Chantilly, Virginia. It opened in December 2003 and holds aircraft too large for the Mall building.

questions.q: Which aircraft, the first to make a sustained, controlled, piloted powered flight, is displayed at the National Air and Space Museum?
questions.explain: The museum displays the 1903 Wright Flyer, the first powered airplane to make a controlled, sustained flight. It came to the Smithsonian in 1948 after years in a London museum.

questions.q: Which aircraft was displayed in part in a scaled-back 1995 exhibition at the National Air and Space Museum after a controversy over the original exhibit's script?
questions.explain: The Enola Gay's forward fuselage was the centerpiece of the scaled-back exhibition that opened June 28, 1995, after veterans objected to the original script.

questions.q: In 2014 the National Air and Space Museum began a renovation of its Milestones of Flight hall funded by a $30 million donation from which company?
questions.explain: A $30 million gift from Boeing paid for the renovated Boeing Milestones of Flight Hall, which displays icons of aviation and spaceflight.

questions.q: Where were the Wright brothers' first powered flights made on December 17, 1903?
options: Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina
questions.explain: Four flights were made that day, with Orville and Wilbur each flying twice.

questions.q: How long was the first flight, flown by Orville Wright on December 17, 1903?
questions.explain: Orville Wright's first flight on December 17, 1903, at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, lasted 12 seconds and covered about 120 feet.

questions.q: What was the longest flight of the Wrights' first day, flown by Wilbur?
questions.explain: Wilbur's fourth flight of the day lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet, the longest of December 17, 1903. Strong winds then damaged the Flyer, and it never flew again.

questions.q: Who built the engine of the 1903 Flyer in about six weeks?
options: Charlie Taylor, the brothers' shop mechanic
questions.explain: Charlie Taylor, the mechanic in the Wrights' bicycle shop, built their lightweight engine in about six weeks. It had an aluminum block and produced about 12 horsepower.

questions.q: How did the Wrights control their aircraft's roll, an idea Wilbur got from twisting a box?
questions.explain: The idea came from his twisting a bicycle inner-tube box in the shop.

questions.q: What did the Wrights build in 1901 to test dozens of miniature wing shapes?
questions.explain: The tests led them to correct the lift data they had been using.

questions.q: What trade did the Wright brothers practice in Dayton, Ohio, before turning to flight?
questions.explain: The Wright brothers ran a bicycle repair and sales business in Dayton, opened in 1892. Money from the shop paid for their flying experiments.

questions.q: On September 20, 1904, Wilbur Wright flew the first what at Huffman Prairie near Dayton?
questions.explain: On September 20, 1904, Wilbur flew the first complete circle in an airplane, in the Flyer II at Huffman Prairie, a field east of Dayton.

questions.q: About how long did Lindbergh's New York to Paris flight take?
questions.explain: Lindbergh's solo flight from New York to Paris in the Spirit of St. Louis in May 1927 took about 33.5 hours and covered about 3,600 miles.

questions.q: Lindbergh's flight was made to win a prize of what amount?
questions.explain: The prize had been offered for the first nonstop flight between New York and Paris.

questions.q: Which San Diego company built the Spirit of St. Louis?
questions.explain: Donald A. Hall was Ryan's chief engineer and helped design it.

questions.q: What political group did Lindbergh support before World War II, resigning his Army Air Corps commission after Roosevelt rebuked him?
questions.explain: Lindbergh was a leading speaker for the America First Committee, which opposed U.S. entry into World War II. He resigned his commission in 1941 after Roosevelt publicly criticized him.

questions.q: What tragedy struck Lindbergh in March 1932?
options: His plane crashed in the Atlantic
His wife died in an accident
His infant son was kidnapped and murdered
questions.explain: In March 1932 the Lindberghs' 20-month-old son was kidnapped from their New Jersey home and later found dead. The case led Congress to make kidnapping across state lines a federal crime.

questions.q: Which woman flew solo across the Atlantic in May 1932, becoming the first woman to do so?
questions.explain: She flew from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in about 15 hours.

questions.q: Earhart received the first Distinguished Flying Cross awarded to what group?
questions.explain: Earhart was the first woman to receive the Distinguished Flying Cross, awarded after her 1932 solo flight across the Atlantic.

questions.q: In 1935 Earhart became the first person to fly solo from Hawaii to which place?
questions.explain: On January 11 and 12, 1935, Earhart flew alone from Honolulu to Oakland, California, becoming the first person to fly solo from Hawaii to the U.S. mainland.

questions.q: Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared over the Pacific on what date?
questions.explain: Earhart and Fred Noonan vanished on July 2, 1937, while trying to reach tiny Howland Island during their attempt to fly around the world.

questions.q: Earhart helped found and became the first elected president of which organization of women pilots?
questions.explain: The group was founded in 1929, and Earhart was elected its first president in 1931.

questions.q: Earhart's 1928 Friendship flight, in which she flew as a passenger, ended in which country?
questions.explain: The 1928 Friendship flight landed at Burry Port, Wales. Earhart rode as a passenger, but she became the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air.

questions.q: Which institute near Tuskegee, Alabama, educated the Black military pilots known as the Tuskegee Airmen?
questions.explain: The Tuskegee Airmen trained at Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, founded by Booker T. Washington. Pilots learned to fly at Moton Field and nearby fields.

questions.q: Who commanded the 332nd Fighter Group of the Tuskegee Airmen?
questions.explain: Benjamin O. Davis Jr. commanded the 332nd Fighter Group in Italy. In 1954 he became the first Black general in the U.S. Air Force.

questions.q: Why were the Tuskegee Airmen known as the "Red Tails"?
options: The tails of their planes were painted red
They flew from Red Tail Field in Alabama
Their squadron emblem was a red fox
questions.explain: The 332nd Fighter Group painted the tails of their planes red, including their P-51 Mustangs, so bomber crews could easily identify their escorts.

questions.q: On March 24, 1945, Davis led P-51 Mustangs escorting bombers to a tank factory in which city?
questions.explain: On March 24, 1945, Davis led Tuskegee pilots escorting bombers to a tank factory in Berlin, a round trip of roughly 1,600 miles.

questions.q: In 1941, Eleanor Roosevelt took a flight with which Tuskegee instructor, drawing public attention to Black pilots?
questions.explain: In 1941 Eleanor Roosevelt took a flight with Tuskegee's chief civilian flight instructor, Charles "Chief" Anderson. Her flight drew public attention to Black pilots.

questions.q: Which presidential order of 1948 ended segregation in the U.S. armed forces?
questions.explain: President Truman issued Executive Order 9981 in July 1948, ordering equal treatment and opportunity in the armed forces. Full integration took several more years.

questions.q: In 2007 the Tuskegee Airmen received which honor at the Capitol rotunda?
questions.explain: On March 29, 2007, the Tuskegee Airmen received the Congressional Gold Medal in the Capitol rotunda, one of the highest honors Congress can give.

questions.q: At Freeman Field in Indiana in April 1945, Black officers were arrested when they tried to enter what?
questions.explain: Three officers were later court-martialed, and the NAACP's Thurgood Marshall helped direct their defense.

questions.q: About how much did Sputnik 1 weigh, a 58-centimeter sphere?
questions.explain: It carried a radio transmitter that beeped for about three weeks.

questions.q: What animal rode on Sputnik 2, launched in November 1957?
questions.explain: The dog Laika rode on Sputnik 2, launched by the Soviet Union on November 3, 1957. She became the first animal to orbit Earth but did not survive the flight.

questions.q: What was the first U.S. satellite, launched on January 31, 1958?
questions.explain: It followed the televised failure of Vanguard in December 1957.

questions.q: Which 1958 education law followed Sputnik's launch?
options: The Elementary and Secondary Education Act
questions.explain: Alarmed by Sputnik, Congress passed the National Defense Education Act in 1958 to fund science, math and foreign-language education. Congress also created NASA that year.

questions.q: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module?
questions.explain: Eagle was Apollo 11's lunar module, which landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Columbia was the command module and is displayed at the museum.

questions.q: Where on the Moon did Apollo 11 land?
questions.explain: Armstrong radioed, "Houston, Tranquility Base here. The Eagle has landed."

questions.q: About how long did Armstrong and Aldrin's moonwalk last?
options: About two and a half hours
questions.explain: Armstrong and Aldrin spent about two and a half hours walking on the Moon, roughly 2 hours and 31 minutes, collecting samples and setting up experiments.

questions.q: About how much lunar material did Apollo 11 bring back?
questions.explain: Apollo 11 brought back about 47.5 pounds, or roughly 21.5 kilograms, of lunar rock and soil for scientists to study.

questions.q: On what ship's deck was the Apollo 11 crew recovered after splashing down on July 24, 1969?
questions.explain: After splashing down in the Pacific on July 24, 1969, the Apollo 11 crew was recovered by the aircraft carrier USS Hornet. They then went into quarantine.

questions.q: What challenge did President Kennedy give the nation in May 1961?
options: To land a man on the Moon and return him safely before the decade ended
questions.explain: In May 1961 Kennedy asked Congress to commit the nation to landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the decade ended. Apollo 11 met the goal in July 1969.

questions.q: Which tragedy in January 1967 killed three Apollo astronauts on the launch pad?
questions.explain: A fire in the Apollo 1 capsule during a launch pad test on January 27, 1967, killed Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee. NASA redesigned the capsule afterward.

questions.q: What was the name of the first Space Shuttle to fly into orbit, in April 1981?
questions.explain: Columbia flew the first shuttle mission, STS-1, on April 12, 1981, with John Young and Robert Crippen aboard.

questions.q: How many operational orbiters were built for the Space Shuttle program?
questions.explain: They were Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis and Endeavour.

questions.q: Which shuttle was a test vehicle that never flew in space?
questions.explain: Enterprise, built in 1976, was a test vehicle used for approach and landing tests in the atmosphere. It never flew in space.

questions.q: On what date did the Space Shuttle program's final mission end with the landing of Atlantis?
questions.explain: Atlantis flew the final shuttle mission, landing on July 21, 2011. The program flew 135 missions over thirty years.

questions.q: How many astronauts died in the two Space Shuttle accidents, Challenger and Columbia?
questions.explain: Fourteen astronauts died: seven in the Challenger explosion in January 1986 and seven when Columbia broke apart in February 2003.

questions.q: On what date did the National Museum of the American Indian open on the National Mall?
questions.explain: The museum on the National Mall opened to the public on September 21, 2004.

questions.q: In what year did Congress create the National Museum of the American Indian as part of the Smithsonian?
questions.explain: The museum act was introduced by Senator Daniel Inouye of Hawaii.

questions.q: Whose collection, gathered over more than fifty years beginning in 1903, forms about 85 percent of the National Museum of the American Indian's holdings?
questions.explain: George Gustav Heye's huge collection of Native objects, gathered from 1903 on, forms about 85 percent of the museum's holdings. It joined the Smithsonian under a 1989 law.

questions.q: The museum's Washington building is clad in which golden stone?
questions.explain: The National Museum of the American Indian is clad in golden Kasota limestone from Minnesota. Its curving shape suggests rock carved by wind and water.

questions.q: Which Blackfoot architect's design shaped the National Museum of the American Indian building in Washington, D.C., though he left the project before it was completed?
questions.explain: Cardinal left the project in 1998, and other architects completed the building.

questions.q: Which cafe at the National Museum of the American Indian serves Native foods from five regional stations?
questions.explain: Its five stations include the Northern Woodlands, the Northwest Coast and the Great Plains.

questions.q: Where is the National Museum of the American Indian's George Gustav Heye Center, which opened in 1994?
options: In the Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House in New York
In a former church in Boston
In the old Mint in Philadelphia
In a former Chicago train station
questions.explain: The George Gustav Heye Center is in the Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House in lower Manhattan, a building designed by Cass Gilbert and completed in 1907.

questions.q: The museum's Cultural Resources Center, which houses the collection, library and photo archives, is in which Maryland town?
questions.explain: The center houses the museum's collections and research programs.

questions.q: In 2022 Cynthia Chavez Lamar became director of the Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian. What distinction did she gain?
options: The first Native American woman to lead a Smithsonian museum
The first Smithsonian director from outside the U.S.
The founding director of the National Museum of the American Indian
questions.explain: Cynthia Chavez Lamar became the first Native American woman to lead a Smithsonian museum when she was named director in 2022. She succeeded Kevin Gover.

questions.q: Who was the National Museum of the American Indian's founding director, a member of the Southern Cheyenne, who served from 1990 to 2007?
questions.explain: W. Richard West Jr., a citizen of the Southern Cheyenne, was the museum's founding director from 1990 to 2007. Kevin Gover succeeded him.

questions.q: The National Museum of the American Indian's 2014 exhibit "Nation to Nation" examined what subject?
options: Treaties between the United States and Native nations
The Trail of Tears in photographs
questions.explain: "Nation to Nation" examined treaties between the United States and Native nations, and how those agreements were made and broken. Suzan Shown Harjo curated the exhibition.

questions.q: Which artist designed the National Native American Veterans Memorial at the National Museum of the American Indian?
questions.explain: Pratt, a Cheyenne and Arapaho artist and Marine veteran, designed it; it was unveiled in 2020 and dedicated in person in 2022.

questions.q: In what year did the in-person dedication of the National Native American Veterans Memorial take place on Veterans Day?
questions.explain: About 1,500 Native veterans took part, two years after a virtual unveiling.

questions.q: By 2014 the Smithsonian reported it had repatriated or offered to repatriate the remains of how many individuals?
questions.explain: The Smithsonian's 2014 report counted more than 6,000 individuals, 250,000 funerary objects and 1,400 sacred objects.

questions.q: What was the Senate vote on the Indian Removal Act on April 24, 1830?
questions.explain: The Senate passed the Indian Removal Act 28 to 19 on April 24, 1830. The House approved it by a far narrower margin on May 26, 1830.

questions.q: Which five southeastern nations, called the "Five Civilized Tribes" by the U.S. government of the time, were removed under the act?
options: Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Crow and Pawnee
Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee-Creek and Seminole
Navajo, Apache, Hopi, Zuni and Ute
Iroquois, Mohawk, Seneca, Oneida and Onondaga
questions.explain: Today these nations are usually called the Five Tribes; the old term reflected U.S. government assimilation policy.

questions.q: Which 1830 treaty, signed on September 27, was the first removal treaty under the act?
questions.explain: The Choctaws ceded their Mississippi lands for payment and land in the West.

questions.q: Which treaty signed in 1835 led to the removal of the Cherokee?
questions.explain: A minority faction of the Cherokee signed it without the approval of the Cherokee National Council.

questions.q: Which 1832 Supreme Court case ruled that Georgia could not extend its laws over Cherokee land, a ruling Georgia ignored and President Jackson did not enforce?
questions.explain: In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that Georgia's laws had no force in Cherokee territory. Georgia ignored the ruling, and Jackson did not enforce it.

questions.q: What name is given to the forced removal of the Cherokee in 1838 and 1839?
questions.explain: The Trail of Tears was the forced march of the Cherokee to Indian Territory in 1838 and 1839, after the disputed Treaty of New Echota. About 4,000 Cherokee died.

questions.q: Which present-day state largely corresponds to the Indian Territory where southern nations were resettled?
questions.explain: Indian Territory, where the Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek and Seminole were resettled, lay mostly in present-day Oklahoma, which became a state in 1907.

questions.q: The Second Seminole War lasted from 1835 to what year?
questions.explain: It ended after thousands of Seminoles were removed west, but a small number remained in Florida.

questions.q: Which Tennessee congressman spoke out against the Indian Removal Act?
questions.explain: The New Jersey senator Theodore Frelinghuysen also opposed it.

questions.q: Which 1887 law, signed by President Grover Cleveland, divided tribal lands into individual allotments?
questions.explain: The Dawes Act of 1887, also called the General Allotment Act, split tribal land into individual allotments. Land left over was sold, and Native land holdings shrank sharply.

questions.q: Under the Dawes Act, how much land did the head of a family receive?
questions.explain: Single adults received 80 acres, and each minor received 40.

questions.q: For how long did the government hold allotted land in trust under the Dawes Act?
questions.explain: The trust period was meant to protect owners from losing their land.

questions.q: Native-owned land fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to about how many acres by 1934?
questions.explain: Surplus land was sold to settlers, railroads and corporations.

questions.q: Which 1898 law extended allotment to the Five Tribes and dissolved their governments and courts?
questions.explain: The Dawes Commission, created in 1893, had registered tribal members for allotment.

questions.q: What was the Meriam Report of 1928?
options: A study documenting fraud and mismanagement of Native affairs
A military report on Wounded Knee
questions.explain: It said the allotment policy had been used to deprive Native people of their lands.

questions.q: Which law of June 18, 1934, ended further allotment of tribal lands?
questions.explain: John Collier was Commissioner of Indian Affairs during its passage.

questions.q: In the 2009 settlement of Cobell v. Salazar, the government agreed to pay how much over mismanagement of Native trust funds?
questions.explain: The 2009 Cobell v. Salazar settlement provided $3.4 billion over the government's mismanagement of Native trust accounts. Elouise Cobell, a Blackfeet banker, led the suit.

questions.q: Which president signed the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act on January 4, 1975?
questions.explain: The law let tribes take over the running of federal programs.

questions.q: In a July 8, 1970, message to Congress, which president called the termination policy incorrect and recommended self-determination?
questions.explain: His message shifted federal policy toward tribal self-determination.

questions.q: In the 1950s, Congress pursued a policy of ending federal recognition of tribes. What was it called?
questions.explain: Termination aimed to end federal recognition of tribes and their special relationship with the government. More than 100 tribes and communities were terminated.

questions.q: Which 1968 law guaranteed much of the Bill of Rights in Indian Country?
options: The American Indian Religious Freedom Act
questions.explain: The Indian Civil Rights Act of 1968 required tribal governments to respect most Bill of Rights protections, such as free speech and due process.

questions.q: Which Mohawk activist emerged as a prominent leader of the 1969 occupation of Alcatraz Island?
questions.explain: The occupation lasted until 1971 and drew national attention to Native demands.

questions.q: Which 1990 law set rules for returning human remains and sacred objects from museums to tribes?
options: The American Indian Religious Freedom Act
The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act
questions.explain: It was among several laws that followed the era of self-determination.

questions.q: Which president signed the Pacific Railway Act of 1862, authorizing the first transcontinental railroad?
questions.explain: Abraham Lincoln signed the Pacific Railway Act on July 1, 1862, during the Civil War. The transcontinental line was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah, in May 1869.

questions.q: Which two companies built the first transcontinental railroad?
options: The Pennsylvania and the Baltimore and Ohio
The Northern Pacific and the Great Northern
The Erie and the New York Central
The Central Pacific and the Union Pacific
questions.explain: The Central Pacific built east from California, and the Union Pacific built west from the Missouri River.

questions.q: At which Utah location did the two rail lines meet on May 10, 1869?
questions.explain: Leland Stanford tapped a gold last spike with a silver hammer.

questions.q: Which group of workers was hired in large numbers by the Central Pacific starting in 1865?
questions.explain: Chinese workers eventually made up most of the Central Pacific's workforce, and they struck for better pay in 1867.

questions.q: Which groups made up much of the Union Pacific's workforce?
options: Discharged Civil War soldiers and Irish immigrants
questions.explain: Union Pacific crews were largely Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans. The company broke ground at Omaha in December 1863 but laid its first rails there in July 1865.

questions.q: Which four businessmen led the Central Pacific and were known as the "Big Four"?
questions.explain: Leland Stanford, Collis Huntington, Mark Hopkins and Charles Crocker were the Big Four of the Central Pacific. They grew very rich from the railroad.

questions.q: Which scandal grew from the financing of the Union Pacific?
questions.explain: Thomas Durant, a key financier of the Union Pacific, was central to the scandal.

questions.q: What track gauge did the 1863 Pacific Railway Act set as standard?
questions.explain: The same width later became the standard across most U.S. railroads.

questions.q: In what form did the federal government give financial aid to the transcontinental railroad companies?
options: Bonds, with more per mile in mountainous terrain
questions.explain: The government lent 30-year, 6 percent bonds worth $16,000 per mile on level ground, $32,000 between the mountain ranges and $48,000 in the mountains, and it also granted land.

questions.q: What did the Pullman Strike of 1894 begin over?
options: Wage cuts at the Pullman Company
questions.explain: George Pullman cut wages by about a quarter but did not lower rents.

questions.q: Which labor leader founded the American Railway Union in 1893 and led the 1894 boycott of Pullman cars?
questions.explain: Eugene V. Debs founded the American Railway Union and led its boycott of Pullman cars in 1894. He was later jailed for six months for defying a federal court order.

questions.q: Which president sent federal troops to Chicago during the 1894 Pullman strike?
questions.explain: Federal troops were sent to Chicago in July 1894 to enforce a federal court injunction.

questions.q: Which holiday did Cleveland sign into law on June 28, 1894, during the strike?
questions.explain: Cleveland signed the law making Labor Day a federal holiday on June 28, 1894, during the Pullman strike. It is celebrated on the first Monday in September.

questions.q: On what ground did federal courts order the American Railway Union to stop the 1894 boycott?
options: It interfered with trains carrying the mail
questions.explain: Debs and the union disobeyed the order, and he was convicted of violating it.

questions.q: The Interstate Commerce Commission is described as the first of what kind of agency?
questions.explain: Railroads were the first industry to face federal regulation by such a body.

questions.q: What standard did the 1887 Interstate Commerce Act require of railroad rates?
options: They had to be reasonable and just
They had to be set by the government
They had to be equal for all cargo
They had to fall each year
questions.explain: The Interstate Commerce Act required railroad rates to be "reasonable and just" and created the Interstate Commerce Commission. It did not let the government set specific rates.

questions.q: The Supreme Court's 1886 Wabash decision held that state laws regulating interstate railroad rates violated what?
options: The Fourteenth Amendment's equal protection clause
questions.explain: Congress passed the Interstate Commerce Act the following year.

questions.q: The Hepburn Act of 1906 gave the Interstate Commerce Commission what new power?
questions.explain: It also extended the commission's reach to bridges, terminals and sleeping cars.

questions.q: In what year was Washington's Union Station listed on the National Register of Historic Places?
questions.explain: Union Station was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1969, years before its restoration and reopening in 1988.

questions.q: Roughly how many stained-glass windows does Washington National Cathedral have?
questions.explain: Washington National Cathedral has more than 200 stained-glass windows. One of them, the Space Window, holds a piece of Moon rock.

questions.q: Before its current multi-year renovation, Washington National Cathedral's Great Organ had about how many pipes?
questions.explain: The Great Organ, installed in 1938, had 10,647 pipes before its current renovation, according to the cathedral.

questions.q: What was the name of Douglass's mother, who died when he was about seven?
questions.explain: Douglass's mother was Harriet Bailey, an enslaved woman. He was separated from her as an infant and saw her only a few times before she died when he was about seven.

questions.q: Which book, discovered at about age 12, helped shape the young Douglass's thinking about freedom and rhetoric?
questions.explain: The reader of speeches and dialogues taught him the power of argument.

questions.q: What did Douglass wear for his September 3, 1838, escape from Baltimore, provided by Anna Murray?
questions.explain: Douglass escaped in 1838 dressed in a sailor's uniform that Anna Murray provided, carrying borrowed papers of a free Black seaman. Murray also gave him some of her savings.

questions.q: Who was Anna Murray, whom Douglass married on September 15, 1838?
options: A Quaker teacher in New Bedford
A free Black woman who was his wife for 44 years
An enslaved woman from his Maryland farm
questions.explain: Anna Murray was a free Black woman from Maryland who helped Douglass escape. They married in 1838 and stayed married for 44 years, until her death in 1882.

questions.q: In 1839, Douglass became what in his church?
questions.explain: In 1839, in New Bedford, Massachusetts, Douglass became a licensed preacher in his church. The experience helped shape his skill as a public speaker.

questions.q: What distinction did Douglass gain in 1872 when he was nominated, without his knowledge, as Victoria Woodhull's running mate?
options: The first African American nominated for vice president
questions.explain: The Equal Rights Party's 1872 nomination made Douglass the first African American nominated for vice president. He did not accept it and campaigned for Grant.

questions.q: In which years did Douglass serve as Recorder of Deeds for the District of Columbia?
questions.explain: He had been U.S. Marshal for the District from 1877 to 1881.

questions.q: Douglass served as U.S. Minister Resident to Haiti until which year?
questions.explain: President Benjamin Harrison appointed Douglass minister to Haiti in 1889. Douglass resigned in 1891.

questions.q: What was controversial about Douglass's 1884 marriage to Helen Pitts?
options: She was white and nearly twenty years younger
questions.explain: Helen Pitts was white and nearly twenty years younger than Douglass, and their 1884 marriage drew criticism from both Black and white Americans, including some of his children.

questions.q: Frederick and Anna Douglass's five children included which daughter, who died at age 10?
questions.explain: Their other children were Rosetta, Lewis Henry, Frederick Jr. and Charles Remond.

questions.q: Which quotation is attributed to Douglass?
options: "The only thing we have to fear is fear itself"
"Give me liberty or give me death"
"I would unite with anybody to do right and with nobody to do wrong"
"I have not yet begun to fight"
questions.explain: The line expresses his willingness to join in any honest cause.

questions.q: How much did Thomas Auld sell his rights over Douglass for to Hugh Auld in October 1845?
questions.explain: British friends later purchased Douglass's freedom for more.

questions.q: In November 1864 Douglass returned to which state for the first time in 26 years?
questions.explain: In November 1864 Douglass returned to Maryland for the first time since his escape in 1838. Maryland had just abolished slavery under its new state constitution.

questions.q: After the Civil War, Douglass criticized whose Reconstruction policies and supported Black suffrage?
questions.explain: Douglass criticized President Andrew Johnson's lenient Reconstruction policies and pressed for Black voting rights, including in a tense meeting with Johnson in February 1866.

questions.q: Who called out "bring him in here" to soldiers carrying the dying president across the street?
options: Henry Safford, a War Department clerk who rented in the house
questions.explain: Henry Safford, a War Department clerk who boarded at the Petersen House, called out to the soldiers carrying Lincoln and waved them inside.

questions.q: At the time of the assassination, where did the Petersens and their children live in the Petersen House?
questions.explain: The Petersen family lived in the basement, while rooms on the upper floors were rented to boarders. Lincoln died in a small back bedroom on the first floor.

questions.q: Who was in the front parlor of the Petersen House, grieving, during Lincoln's last hours?
options: Mary Todd Lincoln and her son Robert
questions.explain: Mary Todd Lincoln and her son Robert waited in the front parlor, while Secretary of War Edwin Stanton questioned witnesses in the back parlor.

questions.q: Who bought the Petersen House in 1878 after the Petersens' children sold it, living there for about fifteen years?
questions.explain: Louis Schade, a Washington attorney and newspaper publisher, bought the Petersen House in 1878. The federal government bought the house in 1896.

questions.q: Who later turned the Petersen House into a Lincoln museum?
options: Osborn Oldroyd, a Civil War veteran
questions.explain: Osborn Oldroyd, a Union veteran and collector, displayed his Lincoln collection in the Petersen House. The government bought his collection in 1926.

questions.q: In August 1864, a gunman fired near the Soldiers' Home where Lincoln was riding. What happened?
options: Lincoln was wounded in the arm
A bullet passed through his hat, and he was unhurt
questions.explain: In August 1864 a shot fired near the Soldiers' Home passed through Lincoln's hat as he rode, but he was unhurt. The gunman was never identified.

questions.q: Which event did Booth attend on March 4, 1865?
options: The signing of the Thirteenth Amendment
questions.explain: He was in the crowd at the Capitol, six weeks before the assassination.

questions.q: On the evening of April 14, 1865, the conspirators met a final time to do what?
questions.explain: Booth planned to strike Lincoln, Seward and Johnson at about the same time.

questions.q: What was the date of Richmond's fall to Union forces, just days before Lincoln's assassination?
questions.explain: Union troops entered Richmond, the Confederate capital, on April 3, 1865. Lee surrendered at Appomattox on April 9, and Lincoln was shot on April 14.

questions.q: How many entries did the nationwide competition for the Jefferson Memorial statue draw?
questions.explain: The nationwide competition for the Jefferson statue drew 101 entries, and sculptor Rudulph Evans's design was chosen. His bronze Jefferson stands 19 feet tall.

questions.q: The Jefferson Memorial's interior floor is built of which stone?
questions.explain: The walls are white Georgia marble, and the pedestal is black Minnesota granite.

questions.q: The Jefferson Memorial stands in a straight line with which building?
questions.explain: The Jefferson Memorial, on the south side of the Tidal Basin, lines up on a north-south axis with the White House. The two buildings face each other across the Ellipse and the Tidal Basin.

questions.q: When were the first Japanese cherry trees planted on the Tidal Basin by First Lady Helen Taft and Viscountess Chinda?
questions.explain: The two women planted the first two trees on the north bank.

questions.q: In 2007 the Jefferson Memorial ranked fourth in the American Institute of Architects' list of what?
questions.explain: In 2007 the American Institute of Architects asked Americans to vote for America's Favorite Architecture, and the Jefferson Memorial placed fourth on the list.

questions.q: What year was the Jefferson Memorial added to the National Register of Historic Places?
questions.explain: The Jefferson Memorial was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on October 15, 1966, the day the law creating the Register took effect.

questions.q: On what date was Lincoln's state funeral held in Washington?
questions.explain: A funeral train later carried his remains through seven states.

questions.q: How did Ulysses S. Grant describe Lincoln after his death?
options: "Incontestably the greatest man I ever knew"
questions.explain: Grant had declined an invitation to attend the play with the Lincolns.

questions.q: What recurring dream did Lincoln tell his Cabinet about, according to accounts of his last days?
options: A vessel moving toward a dark and indefinite shore
questions.explain: Accounts of his dreams are part of the lore of his last days.

questions.q: In what year did Congress approve funds to restore Ford's Theatre?
questions.explain: Work was completed in 1968, and the theatre reopened that January.

questions.q: How old was Lincoln when he died at the Petersen House?
questions.explain: Lincoln was 56 when he died. He was born on February 12, 1809, and died at the Petersen House on the morning of April 15, 1865.

questions.q: In 1826, young Frederick was sent to Baltimore to live with the family of which owner's relative?
questions.explain: In 1826 young Frederick was sent to Baltimore to serve Hugh Auld, the brother of Thomas Auld, who later became Frederick's owner.

questions.q: What happened to Douglass's first attempt to escape slavery in 1836?
options: He reached Philadelphia but was sent back
The plot was foiled and he was jailed
questions.explain: Douglass's 1836 escape plot was betrayed before it began, and he was jailed. Thomas Auld then sent him back to Baltimore to work.

questions.q: In 1843 Douglass was attacked by a pro-slavery mob in which state, breaking his hand?
questions.explain: In 1843, during an antislavery lecture tour, a mob attacked Douglass in Pendleton, Indiana, and broke his hand. He continued the tour despite the injury.

questions.q: Douglass returned to Boston in April 1847 after how long a tour of Britain and Ireland?
questions.explain: Douglass returned to Boston in April 1847 after about eighteen months in Britain and Ireland. That December he launched his newspaper, The North Star, in Rochester.

questions.q: In September 1851, Douglass helped fugitives escape in what role on the Underground Railroad?
questions.explain: Douglass's Rochester home served as an Underground Railroad station. In September 1851 he sheltered men fleeing after the Christiana resistance and helped them reach Canada.

questions.q: In 1857 Douglass lectured on which Supreme Court decision?
questions.explain: In 1857 Douglass lectured against the Dred Scott decision, which held that Black Americans could not be citizens. He argued it would stir more opposition to slavery.

questions.q: What did Douglass call for in 1861, as the Civil War began?
options: The enlistment of Black troops in the Union army
The end of the Union blockade
A negotiated peace with the Confederacy

questions.q: In 1892 Douglass revised which of his autobiographies?
options: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
Life and Times of Frederick Douglass
questions.explain: Life and Times of Frederick Douglass, his third autobiography, was first published in 1881. Douglass revised and expanded it in 1892.

questions.q: According to historian Dickson Preston's research, Douglass was probably born in which month and year?
questions.explain: Dickson Preston found plantation records suggesting Douglass was born in February 1818. Douglass never knew his birth date and chose February 14 to celebrate.

questions.q: Who was the second Bishop of Washington, who died in 1923 before the Resurrection Chapel was completed?
questions.explain: Alfred Harding was Bishop of Washington from 1909 until his death in 1923. He succeeded the first bishop, Henry Satterlee.
